About the sample application

The brokerage in this book is fictional. Its customers, accounts and prices are invented, and its market is a simulation. The code is a teaching implementation: state lives in memory, and the authorization server is configured for local development only. It is not a trading system and must never be connected to real accounts, real markets or real credentials.

Standards and third-party APIs

The RFCs, Internet-Drafts and specifications cited here are the normative sources; where this book and a specification disagree, the specification governs. Chapter 24 describes the publicly documented Webull OpenAPI as of September 2026, for comparison only. Product features, model names and draft standards change, so check current documentation before relying on them.

Preface

About this book

Most APIs that call themselves RESTful stop at JSON over HTTP. This book goes the whole way, and shows with one complete, tested application why the last steps are the ones that pay.

Who this book is for

You write or review HTTP APIs, probably in Java, and you want them to be boringly predictable: every error shaped the same way, every retry safe, every collection paged the same way, and clients that do not break when the server changes. You might be a developer building your first public API, an architect writing your organization's API guidelines, or a tech lead who has to decide whether hypermedia is worth it. You need Java and a working idea of what an HTTP request is. Everything else is explained as it comes up.

What you will build

The running example is a retail brokerage, the kind of API that sits behind a trading app: accounts, balances, positions, transaction history, market data, and orders for stocks and options. A brokerage makes a demanding teacher. Money must never be rounded by accident, a retried request must never buy twice, two devices editing one order must not overwrite each other, and every action must be authorized to the cent. The standards in this book exist because domains like this one need them.

ModuleWhat it isWhere it is covered
auth-serverAn OAuth 2.1 authorization server (Spring Security) with three registered clients and one demo customer.Chapters 4 and 20
brokerage-apiThe REST API itself: HAL and HAL-FORMS hypermedia, RFC 9457 errors, idempotent orders, ETags, cursors, server-sent events, versioning and rate limits.Chapters 5–20
brokerage-clientA small Java client that navigates the API by following links and never builds a URL.Chapter 23
brokerage-agentAn AI assistant built with Spring AI and Claude that uses the client as its tools, with a human confirming every trade.Chapter 25
openapiThe OpenAPI 3.2 contract, served by the API and checked by its tests.Chapter 21

How this book is built

Two rules kept the book honest. First, no code in it is typed by hand. Every code excerpt is pulled from the tested source when the book is built, and Appendix E prints every source file in full. Second, no HTTP exchange is invented. Each request and response was recorded from the running application, against freshly started servers. When you run the same request, you will see the same shape, though prices and timestamps will differ, because the market in the sample application never stops moving.

Light blocks are source code, captioned with the file they come from. Dark blocks are traffic on the wire, captioned HTTP. Long HAL documents are sometimes shortened: a comment such as /* 3 more */ marks where array items were left out, and the HAL curies entry, which every response repeats, is usually omitted. Chapter 10 explains what it is for.

The standard

Chapters that set a rule end with a box like this one. The boxes add up to a complete API style guide, gathered in Chapter 26 as a single checklist you can adopt, adapt or argue with.

A note on the standards

Where an Internet standard exists, this book uses it and names it: RFC 9110 for HTTP semantics, RFC 9457 for errors, RFC 7396 for merge patches, RFC 8288 for links, and so on. A few conventions are still Internet-Drafts, notably the Idempotency-Key and RateLimit header fields. The book says so each time, uses the shape the draft describes, and explains what to watch for. Where no standard exists, as with pagination cursors, the book states a convention and the reasoning behind it, so you can adopt it or replace it knowingly.

Chapter 1

Why API standards matter

An API is a promise made to strangers. Standards are how you keep that promise when you are not in the room: when the network drops, when the server changes, and when the client was written by someone you will never meet.

Tuesday, 9:31 a.m. · a commuter train

Maya taps Buy on 100 shares. The train enters a tunnel. Her trading app waits thirty seconds, gives up, and, because its developers were careful people, tries again. The second request goes through. So, it turns out, did the first. The brokerage now holds two orders for 100 shares, and by the time the train leaves the tunnel both have filled.

That afternoon the app's developers read the API documentation looking for a way to retry safely. There isn't one. They find something else instead: errors arrive as {"code": 417, "msg": "failed"} for a dozen different reasons, so the app cannot tell “insufficient funds” from “market closed.” And a release note mentions that /v1/orders/place will move to /v2/trade/submit next quarter, which means another app release, another app-store review, and another month in which old versions of the app will break.

None of these is a bug in the usual sense. Each is a decision the API's designers did not know they were making.

Every one of those problems has a published, well-understood solution. A client that sends an Idempotency-Key header can retry an order as often as it likes, and the server will create it once. An error written as an RFC 9457 problem document carries a stable type identifier that a program can branch on. A client that follows links instead of building URLs does not care where the server moves a resource. This book is about adopting those solutions deliberately and consistently, so that the next Maya only buys once.

What a standard buys you

“Standard” here means two things. Some are Internet standards: RFCs published by the IETF, such as HTTP semantics (RFC 9110) or problem details (RFC 9457), that thousands of engineers have already argued over. Others are house conventions: choices such as “money is always a decimal string” that no RFC makes for you but that you make once, write down, and apply everywhere. Both kinds pay off the same way.

Without a standardWith oneWho benefits
Every endpoint invents its own error shapeOne problem-details format, one catalog of type URIsClient developers, support engineers
Retries might duplicate ordersIdempotency keys make retries safe by constructionCustomers, and the firm's risk team
Clients hard-code URL patternsClients follow links from one root URLAPI teams, who can reorganize freely
Two devices silently overwrite an order changeETags and If-Match turn a lost update into a clear 412Customers with more than one screen
Each list pages differentlyOne cursor convention and a next linkAnyone who has written a sync job
Documentation drifts from behaviorAn OpenAPI contract tested against real responsesEveryone who reads the documentation

There is a quieter benefit too. Standards shrink documentation. When your API returns 428 Precondition Required, you do not need a page explaining what went wrong: RFC 6585 explains it, every HTTP library knows it, and an experienced developer recognizes it on sight. Every invented convention is something your documentation must teach and your users must remember.

The brokerage you will build

Standards are easiest to judge in a real system, so this book builds one. The sample brokerage has four parts, shown in Figure 1.1, and every one of them runs on your laptop.

The API serves accounts, balances, positions, transaction history, instruments, quotes, option chains and orders. Its market is a simulation: prices take a small random step every second and orders fill against them, so the order lifecycle is real enough to test cancellations and fills. The authorization server issues OAuth 2.1 tokens to three registered clients, each representing a different way customers reach a brokerage. The hypermedia client is a small Java library that navigates the API by following links. The agent is a conversational assistant, built with Spring AI and Claude, that uses the client as its tools and needs a person to confirm every trade.

Why a brokerage? Because it is unforgiving. A social network can show a stale like count. A brokerage that rounds a price, repeats an order or lets two edits collide costs somebody money. If a standard earns its keep here, it will earn its keep anywhere.

How to read this book

The chapters build on each other. Part I sets out REST and HTTP and gets the code running. Part II designs the resources. Part III adds hypermedia, the part of REST most APIs skip. Part IV makes trading safe: idempotency, concurrency control and errors. Part V covers what happens at scale: paging, streaming, versioning, quotas and security. Part VI ties it together with the OpenAPI contract, tests, a client, a comparison with a real-world RPC-style brokerage API, and an AI agent.

The standard
  1. Where an Internet standard exists, use it, and name it in your documentation.
  2. Where none exists, write the convention down once and apply it to every endpoint.
  3. Treat consistency as a feature: the second endpoint should hold no surprises for anyone who has used the first.
Chapter 2

REST in one chapter

REST is not a protocol, a format or a URL style. It is a short list of constraints, and the payoff for accepting them is an API that can change on the server without breaking the clients.

Roy Fielding described Representational State Transfer in his 2000 doctoral dissertation as the architectural style of the Web itself: the set of choices that let millions of independently written browsers and servers keep working together while both sides evolved. An API is RESTful to the degree that it adopts the same constraints. Each one costs you something, and each one buys you something specific.

The constraints

Client–server
The client owns the user interface and the server owns the data and rules. In the brokerage, buying power is computed only by the server. A client can display it, but never decides it.
Stateless
Every request carries everything the server needs to understand it: the access token, the account, the order. The server keeps no conversation state between requests. That is why the brokerage API disables HTTP sessions entirely, and why any instance behind a load balancer can answer any request.
Cacheable
Responses say whether, and for how long, they may be reused. A quote is good for one second, and only for the user who asked (Cache-Control: max-age=1, private). An account balance must never be stored by a shared cache at all.
Uniform interface
Every resource is manipulated the same way: identified by a URI, read and changed through representations, described by self-descriptive messages, and connected by links. This is the constraint that separates REST from “JSON over HTTP,” and it has four parts, covered below.
Layered system
A client cannot tell whether it is talking to the server itself, a cache, a gateway or a rate limiter. The brokerage adds its rate limiting and request IDs as layers that no endpoint has to know about.
Code on demand (optional)
A server may send code for the client to run, as web pages send JavaScript. APIs rarely use it, and this one does not.

The uniform interface, in four parts

  1. Resources are identified by URIs. The order ORD-100002 in account ACC-1001 is /accounts/ACC-1001/orders/ORD-100002, and only that.
  2. Resources are manipulated through representations. The client never touches the order itself. It receives a JSON representation, and it changes the order by sending one: a merge patch that says {"limitPrice": "455.00"}.
  3. Messages are self-descriptive. A response says what it is. For example, Content-Type: application/problem+json announces an error document before the client reads a byte of it, and ETag says which version of the order this is.
  4. Hypermedia is the engine of application state. Responses contain links to what the client can do next. An open order links to its cancellation; a filled order does not. This is HATEOAS, the subject of Part III.

The Richardson maturity model

Leonard Richardson proposed a simple way to see how far an API has gone toward REST, in four levels. Martin Fowler's write-up made it famous. Here is the brokerage's order placement at each level.

Level 0 uses HTTP only as a tunnel: one URL, one method, and the real request hidden in the body. Level 1 gives things addresses but still treats HTTP as a pipe. Level 2 uses methods and status codes as HTTP defines them, so caches, proxies and client libraries understand what is going on; 201 Created with a Location header is a sentence every HTTP developer can read. Level 3 adds hypermedia controls. The response to a new order links to the order, to a way to change it and to a way to cancel it, and the client learns what it may do from the response rather than from documentation.

Levels are not grades. A level 2 API can be excellent, and plenty of successful public APIs stop there. The argument of this book is narrower: the step to level 3 is cheaper than it looks with modern frameworks, and in a domain where actions depend on state and permissions, as trading does, it removes a whole class of client bugs. Chapter 9 makes that case in detail.

Resources and representations

A resource is anything important enough to have its own identifier: an account, an order, a quote, even an order preview. A representation is a document describing the resource's current state in some format. One resource can have several representations. The brokerage serves every order as plain HAL (application/hal+json) and, to clients that ask for it, as HAL-FORMS (application/prs.hal-forms+json), which adds descriptions of the forms a client may submit. The URI stays the same; the Accept header chooses the representation.

This distinction pays off in design. You do not have to expose your database tables. A balances resource can be computed on every request from the ledger and the market, because to the client a resource is whatever the representation says, however it came to be.

What REST is not

  • Not CRUD over tables. The brokerage has no DELETE for orders. A canceled order still exists, so canceling is a state change modeled as a resource of its own: POST …/orders/ORD-100002/cancellation.
  • Not a URL style. Pretty URLs are pleasant, but a REST client must not depend on them. Clients follow links; the server may reorganize its URLs at will.
  • Not JSON. REST is format-neutral. What matters is that the format is described by a media type and can carry links.
  • Not the opposite of RPC. Some operations are awkward as resources. Chapter 24 compares the brokerage with a real RPC-style trading API, and says when RPC is the better fit.
The standard
  1. Every request is self-contained: no server-side sessions, and the token travels with every call.
  2. Every important thing is a resource with a stable URI, including processes such as previews and cancellations.
  3. Methods and status codes mean exactly what RFC 9110 says they mean.
  4. Responses carry links to related resources and to the actions available right now.
Chapter 3

HTTP, the parts that matter

HTTP already defines most of what an API needs: verbs with guarantees, a vocabulary of outcomes, and headers for caching, concurrency and negotiation. Using them as defined is most of the work of a good API.

Methods and their guarantees

RFC 9110 gives each method two properties that clients, proxies and retry libraries rely on. A safe method does not change anything the client is responsible for, so it can be prefetched, cached and retried freely. An idempotent method has the same effect whether it is sent once or ten times, so a client can retry it after a timeout.

MethodSafeIdempotentHow the brokerage uses it
GETyesyesEvery read: accounts, positions, quotes, orders, the event stream.
HEADyesyesLike GET without the body; Spring answers it for every GET mapping.
POSTnonoPlacing an order, previewing one, requesting a cancellation. Made retry-safe with an Idempotency-Key (Chapter 14).
PATCHnonoChanging an open order, as a JSON merge patch guarded by If-Match (Chapter 15).
PUTnoyesNot used: no resource here is replaced wholesale by the client.
DELETEnoyesNot used: orders are never deleted, only canceled, and history is never erased.

Notice what drives the choice of method: the effect, not the URL. Canceling an order is not a DELETE, because the order survives with the status CANCELLED and stays readable forever. It is not a PATCH of status, because a client does not get to set a status; it can only ask for a cancellation, which the market may overtake with a fill. So it is a POST that creates a cancellation request, answered with 202 Accepted.

Status codes: the vocabulary of outcomes

A client should be able to handle a response correctly from its status code alone, and then refine its behavior from the body. These are all the codes the brokerage returns.

StatusMeaning in this APIClient's next step
200 OKThe read or change succeeded; the body is the current state.Use it.
201 CreatedAn order was placed. Location names it; ETag is its version.Store the Location, not a URL you built.
202 AcceptedA cancellation was requested and is in progress.Watch the order until it is final.
304 Not ModifiedYour cached copy (by If-None-Match) is still current.Reuse the cached copy.
400 Bad RequestThe request is malformed or invalid: a missing field, a bad cursor.Fix the request; do not retry as is.
401 UnauthorizedNo valid access token.Obtain a token, then retry.
403 ForbiddenThe token is valid but lacks a scope, or exceeds a delegated trading limit.Ask for more authority, or a smaller order.
404 Not FoundNo such resource for this caller, including other customers' accounts.Stop; re-navigate from the root.
409 ConflictThe order's state forbids the action: it has already filled or been canceled.Re-read the order.
412 Precondition FailedThe order changed since you read it (If-Match mismatch).Re-read, reapply, resend.
422 Unprocessable ContentWell-formed but refused by a business rule: buying power, position, a reused key.Show the reason to the user.
428 Precondition RequiredThis change needs an If-Match header.Read the ETag first.
429 Too Many RequestsA rate limit was reached.Wait for Retry-After, then retry.
Never return 200 for an error. A response like 200 OK {"success": false} hides failures from every tool that relies on status codes: monitoring, caches, retry policies, API gateways and the developer's own debugger. If something went wrong, the status line must say so.

The headers this API speaks

Request headerPurpose
AuthorizationThe OAuth bearer token.
AcceptHAL or HAL-FORMS.
Content-TypeJSON or merge patch.
Idempotency-KeyMakes an order retry-safe.
If-MatchChange only this version.
If-None-MatchSend it only if changed.
API-VersionPin the API version.
Last-Event-IDResume an event stream.
X-Request-IdCorrelate your logs with ours.
Response headerPurpose
LocationWhere the new order lives.
ETagThe version of this state.
Cache-ControlWhether and how long to cache.
Idempotent-ReplayedThis is a stored result.
Deprecation, SunsetThis version is going away.
RateLimit, -PolicyYour quota and what is left.
Retry-AfterHow long to wait.
WWW-AuthenticateWhy a token was refused.
X-Request-IdQuote it to support.

Media types and content negotiation

The Content-Type of every message tells the receiver how to read it. The brokerage uses these types, each defined by a specification you can cite.

Media typeUsed for
application/hal+jsonEvery resource representation (the default).
application/prs.hal-forms+jsonThe same representations plus _templates, on request.
application/problem+jsonEvery error (RFC 9457).
application/jsonRequest bodies for new orders and previews.
application/merge-patch+jsonChanges to an order (RFC 7396).
text/event-streamThe live order event stream.
application/openapi+yamlThe API's own OpenAPI description.

A client picks among the representations the server offers with the Accept header. Ask for an account as plain HAL and you receive its links. Ask for application/prs.hal-forms+json and the same account also describes the order form you may submit, as Chapter 12 shows. If a client asks for a type the server cannot produce, the answer is 406 Not Acceptable; if it sends a body in a type the endpoint does not read, it is 415 Unsupported Media Type. Both come back as problem documents like every other error.

The standard
  1. Choose methods by their guarantees: GET for reads, POST for non-idempotent actions, PATCH for partial changes.
  2. Use the most specific status code that applies, and never report an error with a 2xx status.
  3. Label every body with a precise media type; use registered types and headers before inventing new ones.
Chapter 4

Your workbench

Twenty minutes from now you will have the whole brokerage running on your machine, a token in hand, and your first hypermedia response on the screen. Every later chapter assumes you can reproduce what it shows.

What you need

The code targets Java 27, the release that became generally available on September 15, 2026, so you need a JDK 27. Install one with your platform's package manager or a version manager such as SDKMAN, and check it:

You do not need Maven installed: the project includes the Maven Wrapper, a small script (mvnw, or mvnw.cmd on Windows) that downloads the exact Maven version the project was built with, 3.9.16, the first time you run it. You will also want curl.

If your IDE complains. IDE support for a new Java release often lags by a few weeks. If your editor reports errors that Maven does not, trust Maven, and update the IDE's Java tooling. The book's code compiles and its tests pass with the command-line build.

A tour of the project

The code lives in the brokerage-apis folder of the book's repository. It is a multi-module Maven build whose parent is Spring Boot 4.1.1.

The API's packages follow its domain, not its layers. Everything about orders, from the controller to the idempotency store, lives in orders; cross-cutting machinery such as error handling lives in platform. When you want to know how cancellation works, there is one package to read.

Build and test

From the brokerage-apis folder, build everything and run every test:

The first run downloads Maven and the dependencies, so it takes a few minutes; after that, a full build with tests takes well under a minute. Each module also produces an executable jar under its target folder.

Start the servers

Open two terminals in brokerage-apis. Start the authorization server first: the API fetches its configuration and signing keys from it to validate tokens.

The API seeds two demo customers with accounts, cash, positions and a year of transaction history, and starts a market simulation that ticks once a second. Everything is in memory: restart the API and you start fresh.

Get a token

Every call except the API root needs an OAuth access token. The quickest way to get one is the brokerage-cli client, which stands for a customer's own script. It uses the client credentials grant: it authenticates as itself and receives a token bound to its customer.

The access token is a signed JWT. Its payload carries the claims the API relies on. You can decode the middle section of any JWT with a base64 decoder; for this token it reads:

Three claims matter most. aud says the token was minted for the brokerage API and nothing else, and the API rejects tokens meant for other audiences. scope lists what the client may do. customer_id says whose accounts it may see. Chapter 20 explains where each comes from. For the rest of this book, assume a shell variable holds the token:

Your first hypermedia response

The API root is the one URL a client needs to know, and the only one that needs no token:

Read the response as a menu. There is a link to the accounts, a templated link for searching instruments, a machine-readable description of the API (service-desc), human documentation (service-doc), and the protected resource metadata that tells a client where to get tokens. The curies entry explains the bk: prefix, and Chapter 10 covers it. From here, a client can reach every resource in the API without building a single URL. Follow the accounts link with your token:

Take the guided tour

The client module includes a demo that exercises the API end to end through the hypermedia client of Chapter 23: it lists accounts, reads balances and positions, fetches a quote, previews and places a limit order below the market, cancels it, and waits for the cancellation to complete. With both servers running:

Not one URL in the demo was built by hand. Every request followed a link that the previous response provided, which is the promise of the next ten chapters.

When something goes wrong

SymptomCause and fix
UnsupportedClassVersionError, class file version 71You ran the jar with an older Java. Use JDK 27.
Port 8080 was already in useStop the other process, or add --server.port=8081 to the command.
Every call returns 401The token expired (15 minutes for brokerage-cli), or the authorization server was restarted and its signing keys changed. Get a new token.
Calls with a fresh token still fail with 401The API fetches the authorization server's configuration and signing keys on the first authenticated request. Make sure the authorization server is running on port 9000.
The standard
  1. An API ships with a one-command build that runs every test, and a way to run it locally with realistic data.
  2. Local development never needs production credentials: tokens come from a local authorization server.
Part II

Designing Resources

A brokerage modeled as resources: what gets an address, what the representations look like, and how money, time and identity are written down. Then the read side of the API, from accounts to option chains, one captured exchange at a time.

05 Modeling a brokerage  ·  06 Representations  ·  07 Accounts and history  ·  08 Market data
Chapter 5

Modeling a brokerage

Resource design starts from what users need to see and do, not from database tables. The trick is to turn every verb that matters into a noun with an address.

From screens to resources

Picture the trading app your API will serve. A home screen lists the customer's accounts. An account screen shows cash, buying power, holdings and recent activity. A ticket lets the customer pick a stock, see an estimate and place an order. An orders screen shows what is working and what has filled, with a button to cancel. A quote screen shows the price; an options screen shows contracts by expiration. Each of those is information a client needs, and each becomes a resource.

What the user sees or doesResourceKind
My accounts/accountsCollection
One account/accounts/{accountId}Item
Cash and buying power/accounts/{accountId}/balancesComputed view
Holdings/accounts/{accountId}/positionsCollection
Activity statement/accounts/{accountId}/transactionsPaged collection
What would this order cost?/accounts/{accountId}/order-previewsProcess (POST)
My orders; place one/accounts/{accountId}/ordersPaged collection
One order; change it/accounts/{accountId}/orders/{orderId}Item
Cancel it…/orders/{orderId}/cancellationProcess (POST)
Tell me when things happen/accounts/{accountId}/order-eventsEvent stream
Find a stock/instruments?symbol=AAPLFiltered collection
Its price/instruments/{instrumentId}/quoteItem (changes every second)
Its options/instruments/{instrumentId}/option-chainFiltered collection

Two design decisions hide in that table. First, processes become resources. “Preview an order” and “cancel an order” are verbs, but REST has no custom verbs, so each becomes a noun you POST to: an order preview, a cancellation. This is not a trick to satisfy a style guide. A cancellation really is a thing with its own life. It is requested, it may fail because the order filled first, and it completes later. Naming it makes that life visible.

Second, account data hangs off the account, market data does not. Balances, positions, transactions and orders belong to one account, and their URIs say so. Instruments and quotes are the same for everyone, so they live at the top level. The URI structure mirrors ownership, and ownership is what authorization checks.

Rules for URIs

URIs are for the server to design and for clients to follow, but people still read them in logs and debuggers, so a few conventions keep them humane.

  • Nouns, plural for collections: /accounts, /orders. Singular for a resource of which there is one per parent: /balances (one balance sheet), /quote, /cancellation.
  • Lowercase, with hyphens: /order-previews, /option-chain. Never camel case, never underscores, never a file extension.
  • Nest only for ownership, and not deeply: an order belongs to an account, so /accounts/{accountId}/orders/{orderId}. Nothing in this API is nested more deeply than that.
  • Filters go in the query string: ?status=OPEN&symbol=AAPL, not /orders/open/aapl. Query parameters are optional, combinable and self-describing.
  • No verbs, except as the nouns of processes, like cancellation.
  • No version in the path: /v2/accounts would give one account two URIs. Versions travel in a header instead (Chapter 19).

Identifiers are opaque

The brokerage's identifiers look like ACC-1001, ORD-100002 and OPT-AAPL-261016-C-240. They are readable, which helps in logs and support tickets, but they are opaque to clients: a client stores an ID and sends it back, and never takes it apart. The option contract's ID happens to contain its expiration and strike, but a client that parses them out has written a bug that will fire the day the ID scheme changes. The contract's terms are in its representation, as fields, for exactly that reason.

One resource, one URI; one URI, one resource

Each resource has exactly one canonical URI, the one in its self link. That rule is why the API has no /v1 in its paths, and why an order has no second address such as /orders/ORD-100002 outside its account. Two URIs for one thing split caches, confuse logs and double the authorization rules. When a client needs a shortcut, the server gives it a link, not a second address.

Resources are not tables. balances has no table behind it: it is computed on each request from the ledger and live prices. order-previews stores nothing at all. The API promises what a representation contains, not how it is stored, which leaves the server free to change its internals.
The standard
  1. Model what clients need to see and do; give every such thing, including processes, a noun and a URI.
  2. URIs are lowercase, hyphenated, plural for collections, nested only for ownership, with filters in the query string.
  3. Identifiers are opaque strings; everything a client needs is a field in the representation.
  4. Every resource has exactly one canonical URI: the self link.
Chapter 6

Representations: money, time and identity

A representation is a contract written in JSON. The decisions that matter most are small ones: how to write a price, a timestamp, an absent value. Get them wrong once and every client inherits the mistake.

Money is a string

JSON has one number type, and most JSON parsers read it as a binary floating-point double. In binary floating point, 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004, and a price such as 232.42 cannot be represented exactly at all. A server that writes prices as JSON numbers is therefore trusting every client's parser not to round them. In a brokerage, that trust is misplaced.

So every price, amount and quantity in this API is a decimal string: "limitPrice": "450.00". A string survives every JSON parser intact, and the client decides how to read it, usually into BigDecimal in Java or a decimal library elsewhere. One bean configures this for every representation:

The OpenAPI contract describes such strings with a Decimal schema that carries a pattern, so a generated client knows to expect "187.50" and not 187.5. Counts that are naturally integers, such as a quote's traded volume, stay JSON numbers.

ValueExampleScale
Cash, amounts, market values"32420.55"2 decimal places, rounded half-even
Prices, limits, stops"232.42"As entered, up to 4 decimal places
Average fill price"232.0400"4 decimal places: an average needs more precision than a price
Quantities"10", "0.5"Up to 6 decimal places, for fractional shares
Percentages"29.14"2 decimal places, as percent (not a fraction)
Counts1250184A JSON integer

Every amount also travels with an explicit currency (an ISO 4217 code such as USD) on the account, the instrument or the balance sheet it belongs to. A client never guesses a currency from a symbol, and never formats one into a value.

Time is UTC

Moments are written in ISO 8601 in UTC with a Z, as Java's Instant serializes them: "createdAt": "2026-09-29T10:03:28.574985Z". Calendar dates that have no time of day, such as the date an account was opened or the date a trade settles, are plain ISO dates: "settlesOn": "2026-09-30". The API never sends local times or time-zone offsets. A client converts to the user's zone for display, and only for display.

The distinction matters. A trade executed at 3:59 p.m. in New York is 19:59Z; the date it settles is a business date defined by market rules, one business day later under the T+1 cycle US equity markets use:

Names and enumerations

Property names are camelCase, matching the Java records that produce them one for one. Enumerated values are UPPER_SNAKE_CASE strings such as MARKET, STOP_LIMIT and PENDING_CANCEL. Both choices are common; what matters is picking one and never mixing them. An order written in this style looks like this:

Absent is not null

A market order has no limit price, and an unfilled order has no average fill price. The API omits such fields rather than sending null, which you can see in the capture above. One line of Spring Boot configuration applies the rule everywhere:

Omission keeps representations small and removes a question every client would otherwise ask: does null mean “none,” “unknown” or “not loaded”? Here, a missing field means the concept does not apply to this resource in its current state.

What a representation leaves out

A representation is a public contract, so it should show what clients need and nothing else. The Order record shows three techniques at once:

  • Internal state is ignored. stopTriggered is bookkeeping for the matching engine, and version surfaces only as the ETag header (Chapter 15).
  • Derived values are computed. remainingQuantity is not stored; a method marked @JsonProperty computes it, so it can never disagree with quantity and filledQuantity.
  • Sensitive values are masked or hidden. An account's number is always sent as "****4821", and its customerId is never sent at all: the caller already knows who they are.

Signed amounts and self-contained entries

In a transaction, amount is signed from the account's point of view: money in is positive, money out is negative. A client can total a statement without a lookup table of transaction types. Each transaction also repeats the symbol it concerns, so a statement renders without one request per line.

The tolerant reader

The other half of a representation contract is on the client side. A client must ignore properties it does not recognize and treat unknown enumeration values gracefully, because adding a field or a status is how an API grows without breaking anyone. The book's Java client is configured that way from the start (Chapter 23). It even reads statuses as plain strings, so a status the server adds next year cannot crash it.

The standard
  1. Prices, amounts and quantities are decimal strings with a documented scale; every amount has a currency.
  2. Moments are ISO 8601 UTC with Z; dates without a time are ISO dates.
  3. Properties are camelCase; enumerated values are UPPER_SNAKE_CASE strings.
  4. Absent values are omitted, never null; internal fields never appear; sensitive values are masked.
  5. Clients are tolerant readers: unknown properties and values never break them.
Chapter 7

Accounts, balances, positions and history

The read side of a brokerage API is where most traffic goes. It should be fast, obvious and impossible to misuse, and above all it must never show one customer another customer's money.

The accounts collection

A customer can own several accounts: here, an individual margin account and a Roth IRA. GET /accounts returns them embedded in a HAL collection, each with its own links.

Each account's links are its table of contents: balances, positions, transactions, orders, order previews and the order event stream. A client that wants an account's positions follows bk:positions and never needs to know that the path ends in /positions. The bk:transactions and bk:orders links are templated: the parameters in braces are optional filters the client may fill in, following RFC 6570.

Whose account is it?

The access token carries a customer_id claim, and every account lookup goes through one method that compares it with the account's owner. The comparison is deliberately strict about what it reveals:

Answering 403 Forbidden would be more literal, and it would also confirm that ACC-2001 exists. A 404 tells an unauthorized caller nothing, which is what RFC 9110 suggests when a server does not want to reveal that a resource exists. Because every controller asks the ledger for the account first, there is no path to another customer's balances, positions or orders that skips this check.

Balances: a computed view

No table stores these numbers. The Portfolio service derives them on every request from the ledger's cash, the open orders and live prices, so they can never drift from the books of record:

reservedForOrders is the cash promised to open buy orders: the account's resting order for 10 MSFT at 480.00 holds back 4,800.00. buyingPower is what a new purchase may use, and it depends on the account type:

In the capture, the margin account has 32,420.55 in cash, 4,800.00 of it reserved, so its buying power is twice the remaining 27,620.55, or 55,241.10. The same numbers reappear when an order is previewed (Chapter 13), because both go through the same rules.

Positions: holdings at market value

Each position carries its quantity, average cost and cost basis, and its value at the latest price, with unrealized profit and loss. It links to its instrument and to its quote, so a client can refresh a single price without re-reading the whole portfolio. Every position also has its own URI, /accounts/ACC-1001/positions/EQ-AAPL, for clients that track one holding.

Transactions: the statement

History is the part of an account that grows forever, so it is paged and filterable. It is sorted newest first, and it can be filtered by type and by an inclusive date range in UTC. Ask for two at a time and the response ends with a next link:

The client does not compute the next page; it follows next, which carries an opaque cursor. When there is no next link, there are no more pages. Chapter 17 explains why a cursor beats page=2. Filters combine with paging:

The controller method shows how little code this takes. Note the two expand() calls: the self and next links are concrete URLs, not templates with the unused filters left open.

Where are the transaction links? Transactions are embedded without links of their own. They are immutable entries in a statement, never fetched or changed individually, so the API gives them no separate URI. If a future version needs one, adding a self link will be a backward-compatible change.
The standard
  1. Every read checks ownership through one code path; a resource the caller may not see does not exist (404).
  2. Derived views such as balances are computed from the books of record, never stored beside them.
  3. Collections that grow without bound are paged, with a next link when more exists.
  4. Collection items embed their own links, so clients never assemble URIs from IDs.
Chapter 8

Market data: instruments, quotes and option chains

Market data is shared by every customer and changes every second. That combination shapes its design: global URIs, aggressive but private caching, and links that let a client walk from a stock to its options without knowing a single date.

Finding an instrument

The API root's bk:instruments link is a template, /instruments{?symbol,type}. A client expands it with the symbol the user typed:

Three properties answer the questions a trading screen asks before it offers a ticket. tradable says whether orders are accepted at all, and a halted security is not tradable. fractionable says whether fractional quantities are allowed. multiplier says how many shares one unit controls: 1 for a stock, 100 for a US equity option. The client reads these instead of hard-coding them per symbol.

Quotes: fresh for one second

Two response headers make polling cheap. Cache-Control: max-age=1, private tells the client, and any cache, that the quote is good for one second and must never be stored by a shared cache, because market data is licensed per user. The ETag identifies this particular tick of the market. A client that polls sends the tag back, and while the price has not moved it receives a bodiless 304:

checkNotModified compares the request's If-None-Match with the current tag and, when they match, completes the response as a 304. Returning null afterward is Spring's convention for “the response is already written.” Chapter 19 returns to quotes, because they are the one representation that changed shape between API versions.

Option chains: links instead of dates

An option chain is the list of option contracts for one underlying stock and one expiration. A naive design would make the client compute expiration dates, which are usually the third Friday of a month and are sometimes moved for holidays. Instead the chain offers every available expiration as a link, all with the same relation and each distinguished by its name:

HAL allows a relation to hold an array of links, and name is the standard way to tell them apart. A client renders one tab per bk:expiration link and follows the one the user picks. When a new expiration is listed, the client shows it with no code change.

The option contract

Each contract is an instrument in its own right, with an option object for its terms and a link back to its underlying stock:

Its symbol follows the symbology of the Options Clearing Corporation (OCC): the root symbol, the expiration as yyMMdd, C or P, and the strike times 1,000 in eight digits. AAPL261016C00240000 is the AAPL call expiring October 16, 2026 at a strike of 240. Industry-standard symbols matter because they are what traders, statements and other systems use; the API's own id remains the key for every call.

A market that never stops

Prices in the sample application come from a simulation. Once a second, each stock takes a small random step, option prices follow their underlying, and the matching engine checks open orders against the new prices. Tests switch the simulation off and drive the matching engine by hand, so every price in a test is known in advance.

The standard
  1. Shared reference data lives at the top level; per-customer data lives under the customer's account.
  2. Volatile resources carry an ETag and an explicit, short Cache-Control; licensed data is always private.
  3. When the valid choices change over time, as expirations do, offer them as named links instead of making clients compute them.
  4. Use industry-standard identifiers, such as OCC option symbols, as properties beside the API's own IDs.
Part III

Hypermedia

The constraint most APIs skip, and the one that pays for itself soonest in a trading system: responses that tell the client what it may do next. HAL for links, HAL-FORMS for forms, and Spring HATEOAS to produce both without ceremony.

09 HATEOAS  ·  10 HAL and link relations  ·  11 Hypermedia with Spring HATEOAS  ·  12 Affordances with HAL-FORMS
Chapter 9

HATEOAS: links as the engine of application state

A client that knows only one URL, and learns everything else from the responses it receives, can never offer an action the server would refuse, and never breaks when the server reorganizes. That is the whole promise of hypermedia.

What the acronym means

Hypermedia as the engine of application state is the last of REST's uniform-interface constraints. Application state is where the client is in its work: looking at an account, holding an open order, waiting for a cancellation to complete. The constraint says the client moves from one state to the next by following links and submitting forms that the server put in its responses, just as you move through a website by clicking links rather than typing URLs.

Consider what a trading screen needs to know about an order: whether a Cancel button should appear, and whether a Change button should. Without hypermedia, the client reimplements the server's rules: “show Cancel if the status is OPEN or PARTIALLY_FILLED, and if the user's token has orders:write, and if…”. Every copy of that rule is a place for it to go stale. With hypermedia, the rule lives in one place, and the client asks one question: is there a bk:cancel link?

The order's state machine, as links

Here is the same order before and after it is canceled. While it is working, it offers two transitions:

After the cancellation completes, the transitions are gone. Nothing else about the representation's shape changed:

The code that makes this decision is short, and it is the only place in the system where the decision is made:

Two inputs decide the links: the order's state (isWorking()) and the caller's permissions (canTrade(), true when the token has orders:write). A read-only token sees a working order with no edit and no bk:cancel, because for that caller those actions do not exist.

Links reflect permissions too

The same principle applies one level up. An account read with a token that has only accounts:read and market-data:read does not mention orders at all:

Compare it with the full view in Chapter 7, which adds bk:orders, bk:order-previews and bk:order-events. The client for a read-only dashboard never has to be told that it cannot trade. There is simply nothing to click.

The client's side of the bargain

Four rules for hypermedia clients
  1. Bookmark only the root. Store the API root URL in configuration; discover everything else.
  2. Follow relations, not paths. Find a link by its relation (bk:orders), never by what its URL looks like.
  3. Offer an action only if its link is present. The absence of bk:cancel means “you cannot cancel this, now.”
  4. Store resource URIs, not IDs to rebuild them from. Keep the self link of anything you will need again.

Links are guidance, not security

A missing link tells an honest client what it cannot do. It does not stop a dishonest or out-of-date one. The server still enforces every rule on every request: a client that posts to a cancellation URL it saved earlier, after the order filled, gets a clear refusal.

This is also why hypermedia and caching get along. A client may act on a representation that was accurate a second ago. The server's answer, 409 Conflict with a problem type naming the reason, tells it to re-read the order, whose links will now be accurate again.

Objections, answered

“Clients hard-code URLs anyway.”
Some will. They lose the benefits, and nothing breaks for anyone else. The clients in this book, a Java library and an AI agent, follow links, and Chapter 23 shows that doing so costs no more code than building URLs.
“Links make responses bigger.”
A few hundred bytes of links compress extremely well, and they save the round trips a client would otherwise spend asking what it may do.
“We will have to document the relations.”
Yes, instead of documenting URL patterns, parameters and state rules. A relation is a stable name with a meaning; a URL pattern is an implementation detail with a lifetime.
“It is slower to discover everything from the root.”
Discovery results can be cached like any other representation. A client that already holds an account's representation follows its links directly.
The standard
  1. Every representation links to itself and to its related resources.
  2. State transitions appear as links only when the resource's state and the caller's permissions allow them.
  3. The decision about which links a resource carries is made in exactly one place in the server.
  4. The server enforces every rule regardless of links; a stale link earns a precise problem, such as 409.
Chapter 10

HAL and link relations

Hypermedia needs a format that says, in a way every client can parse, “here is a link, and here is what it means.” HAL does that with two reserved properties and a naming scheme borrowed from the Web itself.

HAL in two properties

The JSON Hypertext Application Language, HAL, was proposed by Mike Kelly and is described in the Internet-Draft draft-kelly-json-hal. Its media type is application/hal+json. It adds exactly two reserved properties to an ordinary JSON object:

  • _links, an object whose keys are link relations and whose values are link objects, or arrays of them when a relation has several targets.
  • _embedded, an object whose keys are link relations and whose values are resources, or arrays of resources, included in the response to save round trips.

Everything else is the resource's own state. A HAL client needs no schema to find the links: they are always in _links, keyed by what they mean.

Link objects

A link object must have an href. HAL defines a handful of optional properties, and the brokerage uses four of them:

PropertyMeaningExample in this API
hrefThe target URI, or a URI template…/orders/ORD-100002
templatedtrue when href is an RFC 6570 template…/orders{?status,symbol,cursor,limit}
typeThe media type the target will returnapplication/openapi+yaml
nameDistinguishes links that share a relation"2026-10-16" on bk:expiration
title, profile, deprecation, hreflangLabels, profiles, retirement notices, languagesnot used

Link relations: the vocabulary

A link relation names the meaning of a link: not “a URL,” but “the next page,” “the way to edit this,” “this order's instrument.” RFC 8288, Web Linking, defines two kinds. Registered relations are short names in the IANA Link Relations registry, such as self and next, with meanings every client already knows. Extension relations are URIs that the API owner defines and documents, which keeps them globally unique.

Extension URIs are long, so HAL provides CURIEs (compact URIs): a named template declared once in curies. In this API, bk:orders expands to https://docs.brokerage.example/rels/orders, a page that documents the relation. Here is the API root again, where the declaration appears:

RelationKindMeaning
selfIANAThis resource's canonical URI.
nextIANAThe next page of a paged collection.
editIANA (RFC 5023)Where to send changes to this resource (a merge patch).
service-descIANA (RFC 8631)A machine-readable description of the API: the OpenAPI document.
service-docIANA (RFC 8631)Human-readable documentation.
bk:accounts, bk:accountextensionThe customer's accounts; the account a resource belongs to.
bk:balances, bk:positions, bk:transactionsextensionAn account's balance sheet, holdings and statement.
bk:orders, bk:order-previews, bk:order-eventsextensionAn account's orders; where to preview one; its event stream.
bk:cancelextensionPOST here to cancel this order. Present only while it can be canceled.
bk:place-orderextensionOn an acceptable preview: where to POST the order.
bk:instruments, bk:instrumentextensionInstrument search; the instrument an order or position concerns.
bk:quote, bk:option-chainextensionAn instrument's latest quote; its option contracts.
bk:expiration, bk:underlyingextensionOne expiration's chain (named by date); an option's underlying stock.
bk:oauth-protected-resourceextensionThe RFC 9728 metadata: where to get tokens for this API.
Prefer registered relations. Before inventing a relation, check the IANA registry. edit, next, prev, first, last, collection, item, related and describedby cover a great deal. The brokerage invents relations only for domain concepts, such as a balance sheet or a cancellation, that no registry could know about.

Templated links

Some links need input from the client. RFC 6570 URI templates express that without giving away the URL structure. The template …/orders{?status,symbol,cursor,limit} uses form-style query expansion: each variable the client supplies becomes a query parameter, and each one it omits disappears.

Variables suppliedExpanded URI
none…/accounts/ACC-1001/orders
symbol=AAPL…/orders?symbol=AAPL
status=[OPEN, PARTIALLY_FILLED]…/orders?status=OPEN,PARTIALLY_FILLED

The client expands templates with a library (Spring's UriTemplate in Java) and never concatenates strings. The server, for its part, sends templates only for things a client chooses. Links a client should follow as-is, such as next, are always expanded.

Why HAL?

HAL is not the only hypermedia format. It is the simplest one that does the job, and it has the best support in the Spring ecosystem.

FormatStrengthsTrade-offs
HALMinimal; plain JSON plus _links/_embedded; wide library supportLinks only; actions need HAL-FORMS
HAL-FORMSAdds _templates: method, fields, validationA separate media type clients opt into
SirenEntities, links and actions in one formatA stricter envelope around every resource
JSON:APIComplete conventions for relationships, sparse fieldsets, pagingOpinionated document structure; weaker affordances
JSON-LD + HydraLinked-data semantics; rich vocabulariesSteep learning curve for most teams
The standard
  1. Representations are application/hal+json; links live in _links, included resources in _embedded.
  2. Use IANA-registered relations where one fits; otherwise define extension relations as URIs, shortened with one CURIE.
  3. Every extension relation's URI resolves to documentation of its meaning.
  4. Templated links use RFC 6570; links meant to be followed as-is are always expanded.
Chapter 11

Hypermedia with Spring HATEOAS

Spring HATEOAS turns hypermedia from hand-written JSON into a handful of types and one link builder. Links are built from controller methods, so they cannot drift from the routes they point to.

Enabling the formats

Spring Boot's HATEOAS starter configures HAL by default. The brokerage turns on HAL-FORMS as well, declares its CURIE, and describes a few HAL-FORMS details, all in one configuration class:

The override is a small workaround worth knowing about. RFC 8631 registered service-desc and service-doc with IANA, but Spring HATEOAS's built-in list of IANA relations does not include them, so without the override they would come out as bk:service-desc: a custom relation, which is wrong. Registered relations must never be prefixed.

Four model types

TypeRepresentsIn this API
RepresentationModelA resource defined by its links, with its own propertiesThe API root
EntityModel<T>A domain object plus linksAn account, an order, a quote
CollectionModel<T>Items (embedded) plus linksAccounts, positions, orders
PagedModel<T>A page of items with page metadataNot used: pages here are cursors

Domain records stay free of web concerns: Order knows nothing about links. The @Relation annotation on a record names it inside _embedded (orders, which the CURIE provider turns into bk:orders), and nothing else about the record needs to change.

Links from methods, not strings

WebMvcLinkBuilder builds links by calling the controller method they point to, on a proxy that records the call instead of executing it:

The builder reads the method's mapping, fills in the path variables from the arguments, adds any query parameters, and produces an absolute URI based on the current request. Arguments that are not part of the URI, such as the request body or the Jwt, are passed as null. If someone renames the route, every link to it follows; if someone deletes the method, the links stop compiling. Absolute URIs are derived from the incoming request, so behind a proxy you set server.forward-headers-strategy to have Spring honor the X-Forwarded-* or Forwarded headers.

The root: a resource that is all links

Three links point outside the controllers: the OpenAPI document, the documentation site and the protected resource metadata. For those, Link.of(href, rel) takes the URI directly.

Assemblers: one place for the link rules

When a resource appears in several responses, its links should be built in one place. The brokerage uses an assembler class for orders (you saw it in Chapter 9) and a method on the controller for accounts, whose links depend on the caller's scopes:

andAffordance(afford(...)) attaches a description of the placeOrder operation to the bk:orders link. Plain HAL ignores it; HAL-FORMS renders it as a template, as the next chapter shows.

Collections and embedded items

A collection is a CollectionModel of item models, each carrying its own links:

Testing the links

Links are part of the contract, so they are tested like any other output. This test checks that links follow the token's scopes, and that a HAL-FORMS client sees the order template:

The standard
  1. Build links from controller methods, never from string templates, so routes and links cannot diverge.
  2. Keep domain types free of links; wrap them in models at the edge.
  3. Put each resource's link rules in one assembler or method, and test them.
  4. Registered relations are never prefixed with a CURIE.
Chapter 12

Affordances with HAL-FORMS

A link tells a client where it can go. An affordance tells it what it can do there: which method to use, what to send, and which values are allowed. HAL-FORMS adds exactly that to HAL.

From links to forms

A plain HAL link to bk:cancel says an action exists. It does not say whether to use POST or DELETE, or what body to send. Documentation fills that gap for people, but a generic client, or an AI agent, benefits from a machine-readable answer. HAL-FORMS, a specification by Mike Amundsen with the media type application/prs.hal-forms+json, supplies it: an extra _templates object whose entries describe the requests a client may send.

Clients opt in with the Accept header. Ask for the working order that way:

Reading a template

MemberMeaning
methodThe HTTP method to use.
contentTypeThe body's media type, application/json when absent. Here, a merge patch.
targetWhere to send it. When absent, the resource's own self URI.
propertiesThe fields: name, required, regex, type, min/max, options.

replaceOrder has no target, so it applies to the order itself, and its contentType is application/merge-patch+json, taken from what the controller method consumes. Its properties are the fields of a change, with the pattern every decimal must match. cancelOrder is a POST with no fields. A filled or canceled order has no templates at all, for the same reason it has no links.

The account carries two templates for a trading token. placeOrder comes from the explicit affordance in Chapter 11. previewOrder appears on its own: Spring HATEOAS records an affordance for the handler method behind every link built with linkTo(methodOn(...)), and HAL-FORMS renders a template for each one that is not a GET. The bk:order-previews link points at a POST handler, so it brings its template along. Here is one of the placeOrder template's properties, from the same capture:

Where the template comes from

Spring HATEOAS derives each property from the request type of the handler method, the class bound with @RequestBody. Bean Validation annotations become constraints: @NotNull and @NotBlank become required, @Size becomes min and max, and @Pattern becomes regex.

The remaining details come from configuration: the list of allowed values for each enumeration, and a pattern that describes a decimal-as-string:

A JavaBean, on purpose. OrderRequest is a class with getters and setters, not a record. Spring HATEOAS decides whether a property is writable by looking for a setter, and a record has none, so every field of a record-based request would be rendered readOnly, a template no client could fill in. The class Javadoc says so, to save the next developer from “simplifying” it. Similarly, @InputType("text") stops Spring HATEOAS from describing a BigDecimal as a number input, which would contradict the API's decimals-as-strings rule.

What clients do with templates

  • Generic user interfaces render a form per template: a dropdown for options, a validated text box for regex, a required marker. When the server adds a field, the form grows without a client release.
  • Client-side validation uses the same rules the server enforces, stated once.
  • Agents and tools learn the shape of an action at run time. A tool-using model can be given a template instead of a hand-written parameter list.

Templates describe the shape of a request, not every business rule. A limit order needs a limit price, and a sale needs shares to sell; those rules involve several fields or the account's state, so the server checks them and reports violations as problems (Chapter 16). The template narrows the space of wrong requests; it does not replace validation.

The standard
  1. Offer application/prs.hal-forms+json beside HAL; describe every state-changing action as a template.
  2. Derive templates from the request types and their validation annotations, so forms and validation cannot disagree.
  3. A template appears only when its action is available, exactly like its link.
  4. Templates describe shape; the server still validates everything.
Part IV

Trading Safely

Orders move money, so every weakness in an API becomes somebody's loss. This part places orders through layered validation, makes retries harmless with idempotency keys, stops concurrent edits from colliding, and turns every failure into a precise, documented problem.

13 Placing orders  ·  14 Idempotency  ·  15 Changing and canceling orders  ·  16 Problem details
Chapter 13

Placing orders

Placing an order is the most consequential request a brokerage API accepts. The design goal is simple to state: a well-formed, permitted order is accepted in one round trip, and anything else is refused with a reason a program can act on.

The order request

An order names an instrument, a side, a type, a quantity and, depending on the type, prices. The four order types behave as they do at any US broker:

TypeExecutesPrices required
MARKETImmediately, at the best available price: the ask when buying, the bid when selling.none
LIMITOnly at the limit price or better.limitPrice
STOPAs a market order once the last price reaches the stop.stopPrice
STOP_LIMITAs a limit order once the last price reaches the stop.both

timeInForce is DAY (the default) or GTC, good till canceled. clientOrderId is the caller's own reference, up to 64 safe characters, which the API stores and echoes but never interprets. Options use the same request: the instrument decides the multiplier and the commission. Fractional quantities are accepted only for market orders on fractionable stocks.

Preview first

A good trading screen shows the estimated cost before the customer commits. That estimate is a resource of its own, an order preview, computed by exactly the rules that placing the order will apply, and stored nowhere:

An acceptable preview carries a bk:place-order link: the next step, offered only when it would succeed and only to a caller allowed to trade. A preview that breaks a business rule is still a successful response. The preview itself worked; the answer is “no,” with each issue carrying the same problem type that placing the order would return:

For an option, the same request shape yields option economics: two contracts at 3.10 control 200 shares, so the notional is 620.00, plus a commission of 0.65 per contract.

Placing the order: 201 Created

Everything in that response has a job. 201 Created says a new resource exists. Location says where, and it is the URI the client should keep. ETag is the order's version, needed to change it later (Chapter 15). Idempotent-Replayed: false says this request created the order rather than replaying an earlier result (Chapter 14). The body is the order itself, with its links, so the client needs no second request to display it.

Five layers of refusal

An order can be wrong in five different ways, and each is caught by a different layer with a different status code. Keeping the layers distinct is what lets a client react sensibly.

Layers 1 and 2: the request itself

A value of the wrong type never reaches the controller; Jackson rejects it while reading the body. The API reports it in the same errors shape as any other invalid field, so a client has one format to handle:

Field rules come from Bean Validation annotations on OrderRequest, which you met in Chapter 12. Every failing field is reported at once, sorted by field name, so a user can fix them all in one pass:

Layers 3 and 4: the rules

Rules that involve several fields, or the account, live in OrderService. Consistency between type and prices is still a malformed request, so it is a 400:

Rules about the account's state are different in kind. The request is valid; the account simply cannot do it. That is 422 Unprocessable Content, with the numbers a client needs in extension members:

All of these checks live in one method, used by both previews and placements, so a preview can never promise what placement will refuse:

Execution

A new order starts OPEN. Each second the matching engine looks at every working order. A buy executes at the ask and a sell at the bid, never beyond a limit, and never for more than the size displayed at that price, which is how partial fills happen. Every execution is booked to the ledger as a trade with a T+1 settlement date, and published as an event.

The standard
  1. Offer a preview resource that applies exactly the rules placement applies, and link from an acceptable preview to placement.
  2. A new order returns 201 Created with Location, ETag and the full representation.
  3. Malformed or invalid requests are 400 with every field error listed; valid requests the account cannot honor are 422; exceeding delegated authority is 403.
  4. Every rule lives in one server-side method shared by every path that needs it.
Chapter 14

Idempotency: retries that can never buy twice

Networks fail in the middle of requests. When they do, the client cannot know whether its order was placed. An idempotency key turns that uncertainty from a hazard into a non-event.

The problem with a timeout

Remember Maya's train from Chapter 1. When a POST times out, one of three things has happened, and the client cannot tell which:

GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition, so retrying them is always safe. POST is not, and placing an order must be a POST, because each order is new. The fix is to let the client make any particular POST idempotent by naming it.

The Idempotency-Key header

The IETF HTTP APIs working group's Internet-Draft The Idempotency-Key HTTP Header Field standardizes a practice that payment APIs have used for years. The client generates a unique key, a UUID works well, and sends it with the request. The server remembers the key along with the result. If the same key arrives again, the server returns the stored result instead of doing the work again.

  • Same key, same request: the original order, marked Idempotent-Replayed: true.
  • Same key, different request: a client bug; refused with 422 rather than guessed at.
  • No key: refused with 400. In this API every new order must be retry-safe.

How the server remembers

Recognizing “the same request” needs a definition. OrderRequest computes a fingerprint from its normalized fields. Quantities are stripped of trailing zeros, so "10" and "10.00" count as the same order, and the default time in force is filled in:

The key store keeps each key for 24 hours, scoped to the client and the account, so two different applications can never collide on a key:

The placement method checks the key before anything else, and records it only after the order exists:

In production. This store is an in-memory map, and the service is synchronized, so two concurrent requests with one key can never both succeed. A real deployment runs several instances, so the store belongs in a shared database, and the key must be claimed atomically before the order is created. A unique constraint on (client, account, key) is the usual tool. The draft specifies 409 Conflict for a request that arrives while an earlier one with the same key is still in flight.

The client's half

An idempotency key is only useful if the client reuses it on retries. The book's client generates one key per order and retries timeouts and transient failures with that same key:

  • Retry network failures and transient statuses (429, 502, 503, 504), never 400s or 422s.
  • Honor Retry-After when the server sends it; otherwise back off progressively.
  • Generate the key when the user presses Buy, not when the request is sent, so that every retry, even after an app restart, carries the same key.

Is clientOrderId enough?

Many brokerage APIs, including the RPC-style one compared in Chapter 24, deduplicate on a client-supplied order ID instead. It is a workable idea: the ID must be unique per account, so a retry with the same ID cannot create a second order. The Idempotency-Key header is the more general version of the same idea. It works for any POST, not only orders; it separates “my reference for this order” from “this attempt”; and it defines what a replay returns, which a unique-ID rule usually leaves unsaid.

The standard
  1. Every non-idempotent request that creates something valuable requires an Idempotency-Key.
  2. The same key and request replay the original response, marked Idempotent-Replayed: true; the same key with a different request is 422.
  3. Keys are scoped to the client and retained for at least 24 hours; claim them atomically.
  4. Clients generate the key once per user intent and reuse it on every retry.
Chapter 15

Changing and canceling orders

A working order is shared state: the customer's phone, their laptop and the exchange can all touch it at once. HTTP's conditional requests keep those writers from silently overwriting each other, and 202 Accepted tells the truth about cancels that take time.

The lost update

Maya's phone and laptop both show her open order for 10 MSFT at 450.00. On the laptop she raises the limit to 455.00. A moment later, on the phone, which still shows the old order, she cuts the quantity to 8. Without protection, the phone's request is applied to an order it has never seen, and nobody is told.

ETags and If-Match

Every order carries a strong entity tag that changes whenever the order does:

A client that changes an order must send the tag of the version it saw in If-Match. The server compares it with the current tag before applying anything. The API goes one step further than HTTP requires and makes the header mandatory: a change without If-Match is refused with 428 Precondition Required, defined for exactly this purpose by RFC 6585.

The currentEtag extension member saves the phone a guess: it can re-read the order, show the user what changed, and let them decide.

Merge patch: sending only what changes

The change itself is a JSON merge patch (RFC 7396), sent as application/merge-patch+json. A merge patch is a partial document: each member present replaces the same member of the resource, and members that are absent stay as they are. That makes the request both minimal and self-evident: {"limitPrice": "455.00"} changes the limit price and nothing else.

Only a working order's quantity, prices and time in force can change. The instrument, side and type cannot. A different instrument is a different order, so the client cancels and places a new one. The server re-runs the business rules on the new terms, discounting the cash the order had already reserved:

Polling cheaply with If-None-Match

The same tag makes polling almost free. A client that has an order sends its tag in If-None-Match. While nothing has changed, the answer is a bodiless 304 Not Modified:

Canceling: 202 Accepted

On a real exchange, a cancel is a request, not a command. It travels to the market, and a fill may arrive first. The API models that honestly. A cancellation request is accepted at once with 202 Accepted, the order moves to PENDING_CANCEL, and Location points at the order, whose status will settle:

Notice that the edit and bk:cancel links are already gone: a pending cancel cannot be changed or canceled again. On the matching engine's next pass, the order becomes CANCELLED, unless a fill wins the race, in which case it becomes FILLED and the cancel is moot. You saw the final state in Chapter 9.

Asking twice is harmless: a second request while the cancel is pending returns the same pending order, so a client can retry a cancel without an idempotency key. Once the order is final, the request is refused with 409 Conflict.

Why not DELETE?

DELETE /orders/ORD-100002 reads naturally, but it promises the wrong thing: that the resource will be gone. A canceled order must remain readable for the customer's records, for regulators, and for the client that asked. Modeling the cancellation as its own resource keeps every guarantee true: the order is never deleted, the request is accepted rather than completed, and the final state is visible on the order itself.

The standard
  1. Every mutable resource has a strong ETag; changes require If-Match (428 without, 412 when stale, with the current tag in the problem).
  2. Partial updates are JSON merge patches with application/merge-patch+json.
  3. Operations that complete later answer 202 Accepted with a Location to watch.
  4. Records that must be kept are never deleted; ending them is a state change.
Chapter 16

Problem details: errors as RFC 9457 documents

An error response is an API's most important documentation, because it is the one a developer reads when something is already wrong. RFC 9457 gives every error the same shape, and a stable identifier that code can depend on.

Anatomy of a problem

RFC 9457, Problem Details for HTTP APIs, replaced RFC 7807 in 2023 and defines the media type application/problem+json. Every error from the brokerage API is one:

The most important rule is the division of labor. Code branches on type, never on title or detail, which are prose and may be reworded or translated. The type is a URI, so it is globally unique. In this API it also resolves to a page that documents the problem: what it means, when it happens, and what to do about it.

A catalog, not a free-for-all

Every problem the API can return is declared in one enumeration, with its type, status and title. There is no other way to produce an error, so the catalog is complete by construction:

Appendix B lists each type with what a client should do about it. Business code raises an ApiException with a type, a detail and any extension members:

One handler for every error

A single @RestControllerAdvice turns every exception into a problem document, adding the request path as instance and the request ID for support:

The class extends Spring's ResponseEntityExceptionHandler, which already renders Spring's own exceptions, such as 405, 406 and 415, as problem details. Two overrides give invalid input the API's consistent errors array, whether Bean Validation rejected a field or Jackson could not read it:

Security errors are problems too

Authentication and authorization failures happen in Spring Security's filter chain, before any controller runs, and by default they produce an empty body. The API keeps what Spring Security does well, the standard WWW-Authenticate challenge of RFC 6750, and adds the problem document by handing the exception to the same MVC exception handling:

Three statuses, three meanings. 401: I do not know who you are; get a token (the challenge even says where, through the resource_metadata parameter of RFC 9728). 403: I know who you are, and your token does not allow this. 404: as far as you are concerned, it does not exist, which is also the answer for another customer's account.

Request IDs

Every response carries an X-Request-Id, and every problem repeats it as requestId. A client may supply its own ID so that its logs and the server's share one value. The server accepts only IDs that are short and plain, so the header cannot be used to inject text into logs:

What never goes in a problem

  • Stack traces, exception class names, SQL, file paths or server names.
  • Anything that confirms the existence of a resource the caller may not see.
  • Secrets, tokens or the full contents of the request.

An unexpected exception becomes a generic 500 problem with a request ID, and the details go to the server's log, where the request ID finds them.

The standard
  1. Every error is application/problem+json with type, title, status, detail and instance.
  2. Problem types are stable URIs from one catalog, each documented; clients branch on type only.
  3. Facts a client needs travel as typed extension members; invalid fields are listed in one errors array.
  4. 401 carries a WWW-Authenticate challenge; 401, 403 and 404 are used precisely.
  5. Every response and problem carries a request ID; no problem reveals internals.
Part V

Operating at Scale

An API that works for one developer on a laptop must also work for thousands of clients over years. Collections that never end, events that must not be missed, versions that must be retired, quotas that must be shared, and tokens that must be trusted.

17 Collections  ·  18 Live order events  ·  19 Evolution and quotas  ·  20 Security
Chapter 17

Collections: pagination, filtering and caching

A collection that can grow forever needs three things: a way to read it in pieces that never skip or repeat, a way to ask for less of it, and a way to avoid reading it again when nothing has changed.

Why not page=2?

Offset pagination (?page=2&size=25, or ?offset=25) is easy to build and wrong for any list that changes while it is read. A statement is newest first, so every new transaction is inserted at the top. If one arrives between a client's request for page 1 and its request for page 2, every item shifts down by one, and page 2 begins with an item the client has already seen. If an item is removed, one is skipped instead. Neither is visible to the client.

Cursors

A cursor encodes the sort key of the last item returned: here, its timestamp and ID, which together are unique. The next page is “items older than that key,” a question with the same answer no matter what was inserted above. The cursor is base64url-encoded so that it looks, and is treated, as opaque:

Opacity is a promise the server keeps to itself: because no client parses cursors, the encoding can change at any time. A cursor that fails to decode, whether tampered with or from a retired format, is a 400, never a silent empty page. The page size is bounded too:

Following next from the first page of Chapter 7 gives the second, with its own next:
