There is no prev, no page number and no total count. Each would cost the server work, typically a count query over a growing table, and none is stable while the list changes. A statement screen needs “more,” and next is exactly that.

Filtering

Filters are optional query parameters that narrow a collection, and they are declared in the collection's link template, so clients discover them. The conventions are few and uniform:

  • Equality: ?symbol=AAPL, ?type=DIVIDEND.
  • Any of several values: repeat the parameter: ?status=OPEN&status=PARTIALLY_FILLED (a comma-separated list is accepted too, which is what RFC 6570 expansion of a list produces).
  • Ranges: from and to, inclusive, as ISO dates in UTC.
  • Order: fixed, newest first. A stable, indexable order is what makes cursors cheap.

Caching

HTTP caching (RFC 9111) is the cheapest performance work an API can do, because clients and proxies already implement it. The server's job is to say, for every response, whether it may be stored and for how long, with Cache-Control:

ResourceCache-ControlWhy
Accounts, balances, ordersno-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidatePrivate and changing; Spring Security's default
Quotesmax-age=1, privateChanges every second; licensed per user
The OpenAPI documentmax-age=3600Public, and changes only with a release

Spring Security writes the strict no-store policy on every response unless the application sets its own header. That is a safe default for an API full of personal data, and even reference data such as an instrument inherits it:

Where caching is safe, the controller opts in explicitly, as the quote endpoint does (Chapter 8) and as the contract does:

Validation complements expiry. When a cached copy is stale, the client revalidates it by sending its ETag in If-None-Match, and a 304 costs almost nothing. Orders and quotes both support it; you saw both 304s in earlier chapters. Collections do not carry ETags in this API: a page of a changing list is cheap to regenerate and rarely identical twice.

The standard
  1. Page unbounded collections with opaque cursors and a next link; bound the page size and reject bad cursors with 400.
  2. Sort in one stable order; filter with optional query parameters declared in the link template.
  3. Every response states its cacheability; personal data is no-store, licensed data is private.
  4. Resources that clients poll carry an ETag and answer If-None-Match with 304.
Chapter 18

Live order events with server-sent events

A trader wants to know the moment an order fills. Polling can tell them, one wasted request at a time. A stream tells them once, as it happens, and with the right design it never loses an event across a reconnect.

Choosing a push technology

OptionStrengthsCosts
PollingTrivial; works everywhere; cheap with ETagsLatency equals the interval; wasted requests
Server-sent eventsPlain HTTP; one-way push; built-in event IDs and reconnection with Last-Event-IDServer to client only; one long-lived connection per client
WebSocketsTwo-way, low overhead per messageA separate protocol; reconnection and replay are yours to build
WebhooksNo open connection; good for server-to-serverThe client must host a public endpoint and verify signatures

Order updates flow one way, from the brokerage to the client, and each one matters. Server-sent events (SSE), defined in the WHATWG HTML standard, fit both needs. They run over ordinary HTTP, through the same authentication and proxies as the rest of the API, and they were designed with replay in mind.

The event stream

A client opens the stream with an ordinary GET and Accept: text/event-stream, and the response simply never ends. Each event is a few field:value lines followed by a blank line. Here is the stream while a market order for NVDA is placed and fills:

id numbers every event, event names its type, and data carries a JSON summary of the order. The summary is deliberately small, and it links to the full order, so the event stream is hypermedia too: a client that needs every detail follows _links.order.

Event typePublished when
order.createdAn order is placed.
order.replacedA merge patch changed a working order.
order.partially-filledAn execution filled part of the order.
order.filledThe order is completely filled.
order.cancel-requestedA cancellation was accepted (202).
order.cancelledThe cancellation completed.

Never missing an event

Connections drop. When a browser's EventSource reconnects, it automatically sends the ID of the last event it received in a Last-Event-ID header, and any client can do the same. The server keeps a short history of each account's events and replays everything after that ID before streaming new ones:

The controller checks ownership exactly as every other account endpoint does, then hands the subscription to OrderEvents. Note the base URI captured at subscription time: events are sent later, outside the original request, where the current request is no longer available to build links from.

Running streams in production

  • History has a horizon. This implementation keeps the last 500 events per account. A client that has been away longer should re-read its orders, then resume the stream.
  • Proxies buffer. Some reverse proxies hold responses until they end, which never happens here. Disable response buffering for the stream's path.
  • Idle connections die. Load balancers close quiet connections. Streams that may be idle for long should send a periodic comment line (a line starting with a colon) as a heartbeat.
  • One process is not a cluster. Here, events live in memory. With several instances, publish them through a message broker so every instance can serve every subscriber, and replay from a durable log.
The standard
  1. Push state changes as server-sent events over the same authenticated HTTP as the rest of the API.
  2. Every event has an increasing id and a typed event name; reconnects with Last-Event-ID replay what was missed.
  3. Event data is a small summary that links to the full resource.
  4. Document the replay horizon, and what a client should do beyond it.
Chapter 19

Evolution: versions, deprecation and rate limits

An API that never changes is dead, and an API that breaks its clients is soon abandoned. The craft lies between: evolve without versions whenever you can, version precisely when you must, and tell clients well ahead of time what is going away.

Change without breaking

Most changes need no version at all, provided clients are tolerant readers (Chapter 6). These are safe:

  • Adding a property to a representation, or a new link to its _links.
  • Adding a resource, a link relation, an optional query parameter or a new problem type.
  • Adding a value to an enumeration that clients were told to treat as open-ended.
  • Moving a resource to a new URI, for clients that follow links. This is the change hypermedia makes free.

These break clients: removing or renaming a property, changing its type or shape, changing what a value means, adding a required input, or tightening validation. The brokerage has one breaking change in its history. Version 1 of a quote had flat bid and bidSize properties; version 2 groups each side into a price level and adds the day's change:

Where to put the version

StrategyExampleTrade-off
URI path/v2/instruments/…Visible and simple, but every resource gets one URI per version, and every link must know the version.
Query parameter?version=2Easy to add, easy to lose when a client follows a link.
Request headerAPI-Version: 2One URI per resource; links stay version-free; the client pins its version once.
Media type parameterapplication/hal+json;v=2Precise per representation, but awkward in tooling and caches.

For a hypermedia API the header wins, because links must work for every client regardless of version. The brokerage uses the API versioning support new in Spring Framework 7: one line chooses the header, and handler mappings declare the version they serve.

Mappings without a version, which is every other endpoint, serve all versions. A version the server does not know is refused, and the problem lists the ones it does:

Deprecation and sunset

Version 1 is still the default, so that clients written before version 2 existed keep working. It is also deprecated, and every response in version 1 says so with three standard header fields:

Deprecation: @1788220800 (RFC 9745)
The moment the version was deprecated, as a Unix timestamp: September 1, 2026. It still works; it will not improve.
Sunset: Mon, 1 Mar 2027 00:00:00 GMT (RFC 8594)
When it is expected to stop working.
Link: <…/migrations/v2>; rel="sunset"
Where to read about the move.

Because the version is a property of the whole contract, a version 1 client sees the warning on every response, not just on quotes. That is by design: the client, not a single endpoint, must move. Clients log and alert on Deprecation headers, and they pin a version on every request, as the book's client does, so that a change of default can never change what they receive:

Rate limits

Quotas keep one client's bug from becoming every client's outage. The brokerage applies two per-client policies in fixed one-minute windows: default, for every request, and a stricter orders policy for requests that change orders.

A quota is only fair if clients can see it before they hit it. Every response advertises the policy and what is left of it, using the RateLimit-Policy and RateLimit fields from the IETF HTTP APIs working group's draft: q is the quota, w the window in seconds, r the requests remaining and t the seconds until the window resets. To show a limit being reached, these captures come from a second API instance configured with a quota of two requests per minute:

A well-behaved client slows down as r approaches zero, waits out Retry-After when it does not, and retries with the same idempotency key (Chapter 14). A fixed window is the simplest fair algorithm; a production gateway would typically use a sliding window or token bucket, and share its counters across instances.

The standard
  1. Prefer additive, backward-compatible change; clients must tolerate new properties, links and values.
  2. Version the contract with a request header, never the path; unknown versions are 400 with the supported list.
  3. Announce retirement with Deprecation, Sunset and a rel="sunset" link; clients pin their version.
  4. Every response advertises its quota with RateLimit-Policy and RateLimit; exceeding it is 429 with Retry-After.
Chapter 20

Securing the API with OAuth 2.1

A brokerage API must answer two questions on every request: who is this client acting for, and what has it been allowed to do? OAuth 2.1 answers both with a signed token, and never lets the API see a password.

Four roles

OAuth names four parties. The resource owner is the customer, Alice. The client is the software acting for her: a web app, her own script, an AI agent. The authorization server authenticates her, asks her consent, and issues tokens. The resource server is the brokerage API, which accepts tokens and enforces what they allow. OAuth 2.1, an IETF draft that consolidates a decade of OAuth 2.0 security guidance, removes the risky parts of the original: no implicit grant, no password grant, PKCE for every authorization code, exact redirect URI matching, and refresh tokens that are rotated or bound to a key.

Three clients, three patterns

ClientGrantPattern and limits
brokerage-webAuthorization code + PKCE, with consent; refresh tokensA web app's backend (a “backend for frontend”). A confidential client: tokens stay on the server, and the browser holds only a session cookie. Access tokens last 10 minutes; refresh tokens 8 hours, rotated on every use.
brokerage-cliClient credentialsA customer's own script, registered to that customer, like a personal API key. Tokens last 15 minutes.
brokerage-agentClient credentialsThe AI agent (Chapter 25). Registered to the customer, with tokens that last 5 minutes and a trading_limit of 5,000 USD per order.

The development authorization server is Spring Authorization Server, part of Spring Security 7. Its clients are declared in configuration:

Why the web app is a confidential client. A single-page app running only in the browser is a public client: it cannot keep a secret, and any token it holds is exposed to whatever script runs on the page. The IETF's guidance for browser-based apps recommends a backend-for-frontend instead: a small server that performs the OAuth flow as a confidential client and gives the browser only an HttpOnly session cookie. Spring Authorization Server agrees in its own way: it issues refresh tokens to confidential clients only.

What a token says

The API trusts only what the authorization server signed. Beyond the standard claims, the brokerage's tokens carry two of its own, added by a token customizer:

The two tokens act for the same customer, cust-1001, with different authority. Alice's browser session was granted read scopes only, because that is what the web app asked for and she consented to. The agent may trade, but only up to its trading_limit. Chapter 25 shows the API enforcing it.

The browser flow: authorization code with PKCE

PKCE (RFC 7636) binds the code to the client that asked for it. Before redirecting, the backend creates a random code_verifier and sends its SHA-256 hash as the code_challenge. Here is the authorization request, captured from the sample server:

After Alice signs in and consents, the authorization server redirects back with a short-lived code and the state the backend chose, which it checks to defeat cross-site request forgery:

The backend exchanges the code, proving possession of the verifier and authenticating with its own secret:

When the access token expires, the backend uses the refresh token, and receives a new refresh token each time, because the server is configured not to reuse them. A stolen refresh token therefore works at most once, and its use by an attacker invalidates the legitimate chain:

The resource server

The API validates each token's signature against the authorization server's published keys, checks its issuer and expiry, and checks that it was minted for this API:

Then one configuration method decides, for every operation, which scope it requires. Keeping every rule in one place makes the security model reviewable at a glance:

Beyond scopes, controllers turn the token into a Caller, whose customer ID scopes every query and whose trading limit caps every order:

Discovery: RFC 9728

How does a client that has never seen this API find out where to get a token? RFC 9728, OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata, answers it. The API publishes a metadata document naming its authorization servers and scopes, and points to it from the challenge in every 401 (Chapter 16) and from the API root.

A generic client, or an AI agent, can go from a 401 to a token without any documentation: read resource_metadata from the challenge, fetch the metadata, fetch the authorization server's own metadata (RFC 8414) from /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server, and start the right flow.

Before production

  • TLS everywhere. The samples use plain HTTP on localhost only.
  • Durable, rotated keys. The development server generates a new signing key at each start.
  • Sender-constrained tokens with DPoP (RFC 9449) or mutual TLS (RFC 8705), so a stolen token is useless on another machine.
  • Secrets in a vault, never in configuration files, and never tokens in URLs or logs.
  • Step-up and consent for sensitive actions, and revocation when a device is lost.
The standard
  1. Authenticate every request with an OAuth 2.1 bearer token; browsers go through a backend for frontend with PKCE.
  2. Tokens are audience-restricted, short-lived and carry fine-grained scopes; refresh tokens rotate.
  3. Each operation's required scope is declared in one place; every query is scoped to the token's customer.
  4. Publish RFC 9728 metadata and point to it from every 401 challenge.

Contracts, Clients and Agents

Chapter 21

The OpenAPI 3.2 contract

Hypermedia tells a client what it can do right now. A contract tells a developer, a code generator and a test suite what the API can do at all. A serious API needs both, and they must never disagree.

Links and contracts are complementary

An OpenAPI document describes every operation, parameter, header, schema and error an API offers. It powers documentation sites, mock servers, client generators, gateway configuration and contract tests. It does not replace hypermedia: the paths in the document are documentation of where resources currently live, not an invitation to build URLs. The brokerage's contract says so in its description, and links to it from the API root with the registered service-desc relation, so a client can find the contract the same way it finds everything else.

What is new in OpenAPI 3.2

OpenAPI 3.2.0 was published in September 2025, and 3.2.1 followed as a patch release. The brokerage's contract uses five of the version's additions:

FeatureWhat it does
$selfThe document's own URI, the base for resolving its references, even when copied elsewhere.
tags: summary, parent, kindHierarchical tags: Orders sits under Trading; kind separates navigation from badges such as Deprecated.
itemSchemaDescribes each item of a streaming response, such as each server-sent event.
oauth2MetadataUrlPoints an OAuth security scheme at the authorization server's RFC 8414 metadata.
dataValue, serializedValueExamples that separate the data from its serialized form.

The version also adds support for the QUERY method, query-string parameters described as a whole, and the OAuth device authorization flow, none of which the brokerage needs.

A tour of the contract

The document opens with its identity and a summary of the conventions every operation follows, so a reader of the rendered documentation learns the rules before the details:

Hierarchical tags organize the operations for documentation tools:

Each operation states its required scope, its headers, its request schema with an example, and every response it can produce, including the problem responses, which are defined once and referenced everywhere. OpenAPI's own links describe, at design time, what HAL's links provide at run time: from a new order to reading or canceling it.

The event stream is where 3.2 shines. itemSchema describes each event, and the JSON inside its data field is described with contentMediaType and contentSchema:

Two shared schemas carry the conventions of Part II and Part IV: the decimal string, and the problem document with its errors array:

And the security scheme names both OAuth flows, and where their metadata lives:

Shipping the contract with the code

The contract lives in its own folder, reviewed like code, and the build copies it into the API's jar so the application serves the very document it was tested against:

Design-first or code-first? This contract was written by hand, beside the code, and is enforced by tests (Chapter 22). Generating the document from annotations is the popular alternative, and it guarantees the document matches the code, but only in the details the annotations capture. Hypermedia rules, problem types and link relations are easier to describe by hand. Whichever you choose, the test that compares real responses with the schemas is what keeps the contract honest.
The standard
  1. Every API has an OpenAPI 3.2 document, served by the API and linked with service-desc.
  2. The contract states each operation's scope, headers, examples and every problem response.
  3. The contract is versioned with the code and tested against the running application.
  4. Its paths document where resources live; clients still navigate by links.
Chapter 22

Testing a hypermedia API

An API's tests should exercise what clients depend on: status codes, headers, links, problem types and the contract, through the real security layer. The brokerage's tests run the whole application, in memory, in a few seconds.

One annotation for the whole application

Every API test boots the complete Spring application with MockMvc, so requests pass through the real filters, security rules, controllers and exception handlers without opening a socket. One meta-annotation holds the setup, and it freezes the simulated market so every price is known:

Tests need access tokens without an authorization server. Spring Security's test support builds an authenticated JWT directly, and a few factory methods give the tests the same claims the real server would issue:

Assertions that read like the protocol

MockMvcTester, new in Spring Framework 6.2 and refined in 7, pairs MockMvc with AssertJ, so a test states status codes, headers and JSON paths fluently. This test is Chapter 15 in miniature:

Some behavior needs different configuration. The rate limit test starts the application with a quota of three requests per minute, rather than wait for the real quota of 120:

Contract tests

The OpenAPI document is code, so it is tested. ContractTest loads the contract and the official OpenAPI 3.2 meta-schema into a JSON Schema validator, and checks three things: the document is a valid OpenAPI 3.2 document, its examples match its own schemas, and real responses from the running application match the schemas the document promises.

The second test matters as much as the first: a validation that never fails proves nothing, so the test breaks a copy of the contract on purpose and checks that the validator notices. Then real responses are compared with their schemas:

It found real bugs. While this book was being written, the contract test caught two mismatches that every other test had missed. Jackson was serializing Instrument.isOption() as an undocumented boolean property named option, colliding with the real option object, and the schema for previews rejected the HAL curies entry that every response carries. Both were fixed in minutes, because the test named the schema, the path and the offending document.

Testing clients without a server

The client and agent modules test against MockRestServiceServer, which answers a real RestClient with scripted responses. The client's test uses deliberately odd URLs: a client that built paths would never find them, so passing proves it follows links.

The suite

Test classTestsWhat it proves
HypermediaTest8Discovery, link relations, scope-dependent links and templates, 401/403/404
OrderLifecycleTest8Placement, replay, validation, limits, ETags, cancellation, previews
ProtocolTest9Cursors, versions, caching, type errors, HEAD, event replay
ContractTest5The contract is valid and the application honors it
RateLimitTest1Quota headers, 429 and Retry-After
BrokerageClientTest4Link following, retries with one key, typed problems, missing links
BrokerageToolsTest, GuardrailsTest7The agent's tools and its human-in-the-loop guarantees

./mvnw verify runs all 42 tests in well under a minute.

The standard
  1. Test through the real security layer with realistic tokens; freeze anything random.
  2. Assert on what clients see: status, headers, links, problem types.
  3. Validate the contract against the OpenAPI meta-schema, and real responses against the contract.
  4. Prove that each validation can fail, and prove that clients follow links by giving them odd URLs.
Chapter 23

A hypermedia client in Java

A client that follows links is not harder to write than one that builds URLs. It is a different habit, and three small classes are enough to make it the easy one.

The rules the client lives by

  1. One configured URL: the API root. Everything else comes from links.
  2. Relations, not paths: every navigation step names a link relation.
  3. Tolerant reading: unknown properties and values are ignored, never fatal.
  4. Problems are typed: an error becomes an exception carrying the problem type.
  5. Safe retries: transient failures are retried with the same idempotency key.
  6. A pinned version: every request says which API version it expects.

HypermediaClient: HTTP without paths

The lowest layer wraps Spring's RestClient. There is no method that takes a path to append to a base URL. Every request targets a link the server provided. You saw its constructor in Chapter 19; its methods are equally short:

Errors never escape as raw HTTP. A status handler turns every error response into an ApiProblem built from the problem document:

HalResource: reading links

A response is wrapped in a HalResource, which answers the questions a client asks of hypermedia. requiredLink turns a missing link into a clear message rather than a null pointer, because a missing link means something:

BrokerageClient: the domain, as navigation

The top layer offers the domain as Java methods, each a short walk through the link graph. Read the navigation helpers and notice what is absent: no path, no format string, no URL.

Canceling shows the payoff. The client does not decide whether an order can be canceled. It looks for the link, and refuses without a round trip when the server has not offered one:

The model records are the client's own view of the API, and only the fields it uses. Statuses and types are strings, so the server can add values freely:

Generated clients and hypermedia clients

OpenAPI generators produce a method per operation with typed models, and they are convenient. They also bake the URL templates into the client, which quietly converts a hypermedia API back into a fixed-URL one. A good compromise is to generate the models from the contract's schemas and write the navigation by hand, as this client does in a few dozen lines. For scripts and throwaway tools, a generated client is fine; for anything that must survive the API's evolution, follow the links.

The standard
  1. Clients are configured with the API root only, and navigate by relation.
  2. Clients read tolerantly and pin the API version on every request.
  3. Errors surface as typed problems; transient ones are retried with the original idempotency key.
  4. An action is attempted only when its link is present.
Chapter 24

RPC or resources? Lessons from the Webull OpenAPI

Real brokerage APIs are often designed as remote procedure calls. Comparing one with this book's design, operation by operation, shows what each style gets right, and which standards cost nothing to adopt either way.

Webull publishes its OpenAPI for customers and partners at developer.webull.com. It is a capable, well-documented API that supports equities, options, futures and other asset classes, with market data over HTTP and streaming. It is also a clear example of the RPC style: operations named by paths, each with its own request and response shape. What follows describes the API as documented in September 2026, and it is a comparison of styles, not a review. Details change, so consult Webull's documentation before building against it.

The same operations, two designs

OperationWebull OpenAPI (RPC style)This book (resources)
List accountsGET /trading/accounts/listGET /accounts
BalancesGET /trading/assets/balances/get
?account_id=…		GET /accounts/{id}/balances
PositionsGET /trading/assets/positions/list
?account_id=…		GET /accounts/{id}/positions
Preview an orderPOST /trading/orders/previewPOST /accounts/{id}/order-previews
Place an orderPOST /trading/orders/placePOST /accounts/{id}/orders
Change an orderPOST /trading/orders/replacePATCH …/orders/{orderId}
Cancel an orderPOST /trading/orders/cancelPOST …/orders/{orderId}/cancellation
One orderGET /trading/orders/getGET …/orders/{orderId}
Open ordersGET /trading/orders/open-orders/listGET …/orders?status=OPEN
Order historyGET /trading/orders/historical-orders/listGET …/orders (paged)
InstrumentsGET /trading/instruments/stocks/profiles/listGET /instruments?symbol=…
QuotesGET /market-data/stocks/snapshots/listGET /instruments/{id}/quote

In the RPC style, the account is a parameter: a query parameter for reads and a body field (account_id) for writes. Operations are verbs at the end of the path (place, replace, cancel, list, get), and every change is a POST. In the resource style, the account is part of the address of everything it owns, and the method carries the verb.

Point by point

Authentication: request signing versus bearer tokens
Webull authenticates each request with an application key and an HMAC signature: the client signs the path, query, body and a set of headers (x-app-key, x-timestamp, x-signature-nonce, x-signature-algorithm, x-signature-version, and the host) with its app secret, which never travels. Requests made on a customer's behalf also carry an x-access-token. Signing gives something a plain bearer token does not: a captured request cannot be replayed after its timestamp and nonce are spent, or altered in transit. OAuth's answer to the same threat is sender-constrained tokens (DPoP or mutual TLS, Chapter 20). The OAuth route wins on ecosystem: standard libraries, delegated consent, scopes, and discovery through RFC 9728, with no custom signing code in every client.
Errors: 417 versus problem details
Webull reports business-rule failures with HTTP 417 and a body of error_code and message. The structured code is the valuable part, and it is the same idea as a problem type. The status is the questionable part: 417 Expectation Failed is defined by HTTP for failures of the Expect request header, so generic tools misread it. RFC 9457 over 400, 403, 409 and 422 says the same things in a standard shape.
Idempotency: client_order_id versus Idempotency-Key
Webull requires a client_order_id of up to 32 characters, unique per account, which makes a retried placement detectable. Chapter 14 compared the two approaches: the header generalizes the idea to any POST and defines what a replay returns.
Pagination: pagination_key versus next links
Order lists take a pagination_key, a cursor in all but name, which is the right algorithm. A next link carries the same cursor with nothing for the client to assemble.
Versions: x-version versus API-Version
Both put the version in a header rather than the path. The difference is only the name.
Naming: snake_case versus camelCase
Webull uses account_id; this book uses accountId. Either is fine, consistently applied.

What the RPC design does well

  • Composite orders. One placement request carries a new_orders array and a combo_type, such as a bracket or one-cancels-other group, so linked orders are accepted or refused together. A resource design needs an explicit resource for this, such as an order group posted to /accounts/{id}/order-groups that links to its member orders. That resource is worth designing before you need it.
  • SDK ergonomics. Operation-per-path maps one to one onto SDK methods, and Webull ships SDKs that also hide the signing.
  • Breadth. One uniform envelope stretches across many asset classes and market-data products.

Standards cost nothing to adopt, in either style

The most useful lesson of the comparison is that most of this book's standards do not depend on the resource style at all. An RPC API can return RFC 9457 problems with accurate statuses, accept an Idempotency-Key on every POST, write money as decimal strings, send Deprecation and RateLimit headers, link to its next page, publish RFC 9728 metadata, and describe itself in OpenAPI 3.2. Hypermedia is the step that needs resources. The rest is available to everyone.

Integrating with an RPC upstream. If your firm routes orders to a broker whose API is RPC-style, you can still offer your own clients a resource API. Put the upstream behind an anti-corruption layer: your resources, links and problem types on the outside, translated to the upstream's procedures, error codes and signing on the inside. Clients never see the difference, and you can change brokers without changing clients.
The standard
  1. Choose resources by default; use RPC-style operations only where a resource model is genuinely awkward.
  2. Whatever the style, adopt the style-independent standards: problem details, idempotency keys, decimal strings, deprecation and rate-limit headers, OpenAPI.
  3. Model composite actions, such as bracket orders, as resources of their own.
  4. Hide a foreign API behind your own contract, not inside your clients.
Chapter 25

Agentic AI: a trading assistant with Spring AI

An AI agent is a new kind of API client: capable, fast, and occasionally wrong with great confidence. Everything this book has built, from scopes to idempotency keys to problem types, is what lets such a client act for a customer without being trusted blindly.

What the agent does

The brokerage-agent module is a console assistant for one customer. Ask it about balances, positions, quotes or open orders, and it answers from live data. Ask it to buy or sell, and it checks the price, previews the order and proposes it, with an estimate and a confirmation code. Nothing happens until the customer types /confirm with that code.

Configuration

Spring AI's Anthropic starter provides the chat model; the agent selects Claude Opus 5 and leaves room for tool use and thinking in each response. The agent is also an OAuth client in its own right, with its own registration:

Spring Security fetches, caches and renews the agent's client credentials token, and adds it to every request the hypermedia client makes:

The system prompt sets the agent's role and its limits in plain language. It explains why the agent cannot act alone, so the model can explain it to the customer:

Tools: thin wrappers over the client

A Spring AI tool is an annotated method. Its description and parameter descriptions become the schema the model sees. Each brokerage tool is a one-line call to the hypermedia client, so the model sees exactly what the API allows, and no URL ever passes through the model:

Tools that would change anything only propose. proposeOrder resolves the symbol, previews the order through the API, and either returns the preview's issues or records a proposal:

The human in the loop

A proposal is a closure waiting in memory. The model receives only its code, summary and instructions, and has no tool that can confirm one. Confirmation happens in PendingActions, called only from the console:

Three details make the gate robust. Commands starting with / are handled by code and never reach the model, so no prompt, however cleverly injected, can type /confirm for the customer. Proposals expire after five minutes, so a stale estimate cannot be confirmed tomorrow. And the confirmation code is the order's Idempotency-Key: confirming twice, or retrying after a timeout, can never place two orders.

Defense in depth: the API has the last word

Suppose everything above failed: a bug in the gate, or a confused model that proposes a trade far larger than asked. The API still refuses anything beyond the limit the customer delegated to this client, because the limit is in the agent's token (Chapter 20) and the API checks it on every order:

The agent's scopes, its five-minute tokens, its trading limit and the customer's own accounts are all enforced by the resource server, not by the agent. The agent is trusted exactly as much as its token says, which is the only safe way to trust software that reasons.

Refusals and fallbacks

A model may decline a request. The console checks why the model stopped before reading its answer, and shows a clear message for a refusal rather than an empty reply:

The sample also opts in to a Claude API feature called server-side refusal fallbacks, in beta as of this writing. When a safety classifier declines a request, the API re-runs it on the fallback model Anthropic recommends for that category, instead of returning the refusal. Spring AI has no option for this request field, so a small OkHttp interceptor adds the beta header and "fallbacks": "default" to each Messages API request. It is an explicit opt-in: remove the RefusalFallbacks component to turn it off.

Testing an agent without a model

The tools are plain Java, so the most important guarantee, that proposing places nothing and confirming places exactly once, is tested without any model at all:

Running the agent

With the authorization server and the API running, build the agent and start it with your Anthropic API key in the environment:

Without a key, the console still starts and /status checks the API and the agent's token by calling a tool directly, with no model involved:

With a key, a request such as “buy 5 AAPL in my margin account” unfolds in a fixed sequence. The model calls getQuote for the price, then proposeOrder. The tool previews the order through the API and returns a proposal with its estimated total and code, and the model relays both. The customer types /confirm with the code, the console calls PendingActions, and the order is placed with the code as its idempotency key. The model never touched the order itself.

Hypermedia and agents. Agents benefit from hypermedia more than any other client. Links let an agent discover what it may do at run time instead of relying on stale training data about URL patterns; HAL-FORMS templates are already machine-readable descriptions of actions, close to the tool schemas models consume; and problem types give an agent a precise reason to explain to its user. An API designed by this book's standards is, almost by accident, an agent-ready API.
The standard
  1. An agent is an OAuth client with its own registration, short-lived tokens and least-privilege scopes.
  2. Delegated limits, such as a maximum order value, live in the token and are enforced by the API.
  3. Agents propose; people confirm through a path the model cannot reach; confirmations are idempotent and expire.
  4. Tools are thin wrappers over a hypermedia client; test their guarantees without a model.
Chapter 26

The standard on one page

Every rule from the chapters, gathered as a checklist you can adopt as your own API style guide, adapt to your organization, or argue with in a design review.

Resources and URIs

  • Everything important, including processes, is a noun with one canonical URI.
  • Lowercase, hyphenated, plural collections, nested only for ownership.
  • Filters in the query string; no verbs, no versions in paths.
  • Identifiers are opaque strings.

Representations

  • Money and quantities are decimal strings with a stated scale and currency.
  • Moments are UTC ISO 8601; dates are ISO dates.
  • camelCase properties, UPPER_SNAKE_CASE values.
  • Absent values omitted; internals hidden; sensitive values masked.
  • Clients read tolerantly.

Hypermedia

  • HAL with _links and _embedded; one root URL.
  • Registered relations first; extension relations as documented URIs via one CURIE.
  • Transitions appear only when state and permissions allow; decided in one place.
  • HAL-FORMS templates derived from request types.

HTTP semantics

  • Methods by their guarantees; precise status codes; never an error with 2xx.
  • 201 with Location for creation; 202 for work in progress.
  • Registered media types and headers before invented ones.

Errors

  • Every error is RFC 9457 problem details from one catalog of type URIs.
  • Invalid fields listed in one errors array; facts as extension members.
  • 401 with a challenge, 403 for scope, 404 for others' data.
  • Request IDs everywhere; no internals revealed.

Safety

  • An Idempotency-Key on every valuable POST; replays marked.
  • ETag on mutable resources; If-Match required (428/412).
  • Partial updates as JSON merge patch.
  • Previews use the same rules as the real action.
  • Records that must be kept are never deleted.

Collections, caching, events

  • Opaque cursors and next links; bounded pages; one stable order.
  • Explicit Cache-Control; no-store for personal data; 304 on If-None-Match.
  • Server-sent events with IDs and Last-Event-ID replay; events link to resources.

Evolution and quotas

  • Additive change first; version with a header when breaking.
  • Deprecation, Sunset and a sunset link before removal; clients pin versions.
  • RateLimit and RateLimit-Policy on every response; 429 with Retry-After.

Security

  • OAuth 2.1 bearer tokens: audience-restricted, short-lived, scoped.
  • Browsers through a backend for frontend with PKCE; refresh tokens rotate.
  • Scopes decided in one place; every query scoped to the token's customer.
  • RFC 9728 metadata, linked from every 401.

Contracts, clients and agents

  • An OpenAPI 3.2 contract, served and tested against real responses.
  • Clients configured with the root only, navigating by relation.
  • Agents propose, people confirm, and the API enforces delegated limits.

Epilogue: the train, again

A Tuesday, some months later · the same tunnel

Maya taps Buy. The train enters the tunnel, and the app waits, gives up, and tries again, exactly as before. This time the second request carries the same idempotency key as the first. The brokerage recognizes it, returns the order it created a few seconds earlier, and marks the response as a replay. Maya owns 100 shares.

At the office, the app's developers barely notice the day. When an order is refused, the app shows the problem's detail and branches on its type. When the brokerage moved its order URLs last month, the app did not change, because it had never known them. When version 1 of the quotes endpoint began sending Deprecation headers, an alert opened a ticket, and the move to version 2 was a morning's work.

None of it is remarkable. That is the point of a standard: it turns the decisions nobody knew they were making into decisions somebody made on purpose, once, for everyone.

Status codes and problem types

Every problem type the API can return, what it means, and what a well-written client does about it. Each type is https://docs.brokerage.example/problems/ followed by the name in the first column.

TypeStatusMeaningClient action

unsupported-api-version400API-Version names an unknown version; supportedVersions lists the valid onesPin a supported version
unauthorized401No valid access tokenGet a token (see WWW-Authenticate), retry
insufficient-scope403The token lacks the operation's scopeRequest the scope; do not retry as is
trading-limit-exceeded403The order's notional exceeds the client's delegated limit (tradingLimit)Place a smaller order, or use a client with more authority
not-found404No such resource for this callerRe-navigate from the root
method-not-allowed405The resource does not support the methodUse the method its link or template names
not-acceptable406No representation matches AcceptAccept HAL or HAL-FORMS
order-not-cancellable409The order is final and cannot be canceledRe-read the order
order-not-replaceable409The order is final and cannot be changedRe-read the order
precondition-failed412The order changed since it was read (currentEtag)Re-read, reapply, resend with the new ETag
unsupported-media-type415The body's content type is not accepted hereSend JSON, or a merge patch for changes
idempotency-key-reused422The key was already used for a different requestUse a new key for a new order
insufficient-buying-power422The purchase needs more than is available (required, available)Show the amounts to the user
insufficient-position422Not enough shares to sell (available); short selling is not supportedReduce the quantity
instrument-not-tradable422The instrument does not exist, is halted, or cannot trade this wayCheck the instrument's properties
precondition-required428A change was sent without If-MatchRead the ETag first
rate-limited429The client's quota for the window is used upWait for Retry-After, retry with the same key

Every problem also carries instance (the request path) and requestId. An unexpected server error is a 500 problem with a request ID; quote it to support.

Appendix C

Glossary

Every term in one place, with the chapter that explains it.

Affordance
A description of an action a client can take, such as a HAL-FORMS template. (Ch. 12)
API root
The one URL a hypermedia client is configured with; everything else is reached by links. (Ch. 9)
Audience
The aud claim naming the API a token was issued for. (Ch. 20)
Backend for frontend (BFF)
A server-side component that runs OAuth for a browser app, so tokens never reach the browser. (Ch. 20)
Buying power
What a new purchase may spend: free cash, doubled in a margin account. (Ch. 7)
CURIE
A compact URI such as bk:orders, which expands to an extension relation's URI. (Ch. 10)
Cursor
An opaque marker of a position in a sorted collection, used for the next page. (Ch. 17)
Deprecation, Sunset
Response headers announcing that something is deprecated, and when it will stop working. (Ch. 19)
ETag
An entity tag identifying one version of a representation. (Ch. 8, 15)
Extension relation
A link relation defined by an API owner as a URI. (Ch. 10)
HAL
JSON Hypertext Application Language: JSON with _links and _embedded. (Ch. 10)
HAL-FORMS
HAL plus _templates describing the requests a client may send. (Ch. 12)
HATEOAS
Hypermedia as the engine of application state: clients advance by following links. (Ch. 9)
Idempotency key
A client-generated value that makes a retried request return the original result. (Ch. 14)
Idempotent method
A method whose effect is the same whether sent once or many times. (Ch. 3)
Link relation
The name of a link's meaning, such as self, next or bk:cancel. (Ch. 10)
Merge patch
A partial JSON document whose members replace the resource's (RFC 7396). (Ch. 15)
OCC symbol
The industry symbol for a listed option: root, expiration, C or P, strike times 1,000. (Ch. 8)
Optimistic concurrency
Allowing a change only if the resource is still the version the client saw. (Ch. 15)
PKCE
Proof Key for Code Exchange: binds an authorization code to the client that requested it. (Ch. 20)
Problem details
The RFC 9457 format for errors: type, title, status, detail, instance. (Ch. 16)
Protected resource metadata
An API's RFC 9728 document naming its authorization servers and scopes. (Ch. 20)
Representation
A document describing a resource's current state in some media type. (Ch. 2)
Resource
Anything important enough to have its own URI. (Ch. 2, 5)
Richardson maturity model
Four levels of REST adoption, from one endpoint to hypermedia. (Ch. 2)
Safe method
A method that does not change server state the client is responsible for, such as GET. (Ch. 3)
Scope
A named permission carried by a token, such as orders:write. (Ch. 20)
Server-sent events
A one-way stream of events over HTTP, with IDs for replay. (Ch. 18)
T+1
Settlement one business day after the trade date. (Ch. 6)
Tolerant reader
A client that ignores what it does not understand. (Ch. 6, 23)
Tool (AI)
A function an AI model may call, described by a name and a parameter schema. (Ch. 25)
Trading limit
The largest order a delegated client may place, carried in its token. (Ch. 20, 25)
URI template
An RFC 6570 pattern such as {?status,symbol} that a client expands. (Ch. 10)
Appendix D

Further reading

The standards behind each chapter, and the best places to go deeper. RFCs are at rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfcNNNN; Internet-Drafts at datatracker.ietf.org.

HTTP and the Web

RFC 9110HTTP Semantics: methods, status codes, conditional requests, content negotiation
RFC 9111HTTP Caching
RFC 6585Additional HTTP Status Codes, including 428 and 429
RFC 8288Web Linking: link relations and the IANA registry
RFC 6570URI Template
RFC 8631Link Relation Types for Web Services: service-desc, service-doc
RFC 9457Problem Details for HTTP APIs
RFC 7396JSON Merge Patch
RFC 9745, RFC 8594The Deprecation and Sunset HTTP header fields
RFC 3339Date and Time on the Internet: Timestamps
DraftsThe Idempotency-Key HTTP Header Field; RateLimit header fields for HTTP (IETF HTTP APIs working group)
WHATWG HTMLServer-sent events and EventSource

Hypermedia and REST

Roy T. FieldingArchitectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, doctoral dissertation, University of California, Irvine, 2000. Chapter 5 defines REST.
Martin Fowler“Richardson Maturity Model” (2010) and “Tolerant Reader” (2011), martinfowler.com
HALJSON Hypertext Application Language, Internet-Draft draft-kelly-json-hal
HAL-FORMSThe HAL-FORMS media type specification, by Mike Amundsen, rwcbook.github.io/hal-forms
Spring HATEOASReference documentation, docs.spring.io/spring-hateoas

Security

OAuth 2.1The OAuth 2.1 Authorization Framework, Internet-Draft draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1
RFC 7636Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE)
RFC 6750Bearer Token Usage, including WWW-Authenticate errors
RFC 8414, RFC 9728Authorization Server Metadata; Protected Resource Metadata
RFC 9449, RFC 8705DPoP and mutual-TLS sender-constrained tokens
Browser-based appsOAuth 2.0 for Browser-Based Applications, Internet-Draft draft-ietf-oauth-browser-based-apps
Spring SecurityReference documentation for the resource server and the authorization server

Contracts, clients and agents

OpenAPI 3.2The OpenAPI Specification, spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.2.0.html, and its JSON Schema
Spring Framework 7Reference documentation: API versioning, MockMvcTester, RestClient
Spring AIReference documentation: ChatClient, tool calling, chat memory, the Anthropic starter
Claude APIAnthropic's documentation for models, tool use and refusal handling, docs.claude.com
Webull OpenAPIdeveloper.webull.com/apis/docs, the RPC-style API compared in Chapter 24

E.2 The authorization server

auth-server: Spring Authorization Server, configured for three clients and one demo customer.

auth-server/src/main/java/com/example/brokerage/auth/AuthServerApplication.java64 lines

   1package com.example.brokerage.auth;
   2
   3import java.math.BigDecimal;
   4import java.util.List;
   5import java.util.Map;
   6
   7import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
   8import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
   9import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.ConfigurationProperties;
  10import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.EnableConfigurationProperties;
  11import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
  12import org.springframework.security.oauth2.server.authorization.OAuth2TokenType;
  13import org.springframework.security.oauth2.server.authorization.token.JwtEncodingContext;
  14import org.springframework.security.oauth2.server.authorization.token.OAuth2TokenCustomizer;
  15
  16/**
  17 * A development-only OAuth 2.1 authorization server. Clients, scopes and the demo user are
  18 * declared in application.yaml; this class adds the two brokerage-specific claims that the
  19 * API relies on.
  20 */
  21@SpringBootApplication
  22@EnableConfigurationProperties(AuthServerApplication.Identities.class)
  23public class AuthServerApplication {
  24
  25    public static void main(String[] args) {
  26        SpringApplication.run(AuthServerApplication.class, args);
  27    }
  28
  29    /**
  30     * Who each token is for. A user signs in as themselves; a confidential client that uses
  31     * the client_credentials grant is registered to one customer, like a personal API key.
  32     * An optional per-client trading limit caps the notional value of any single order.
  33     */
  34    @ConfigurationProperties("brokerage.identities")
  35    record Identities(Map<String, String> customers, Map<String, BigDecimal> tradingLimits) {
  36        Identities {
  37            customers = customers == null ? Map.of() : customers;
  38            tradingLimits = tradingLimits == null ? Map.of() : tradingLimits;
  39        }
  40    }
  41
  42    /** Stamps the audience, customer_id and (if configured) trading_limit into every access token. */
  43    @Bean
  44    OAuth2TokenCustomizer<JwtEncodingContext> brokerageClaims(Identities identities) {
  45        return context -> {
  46            if (!OAuth2TokenType.ACCESS_TOKEN.equals(context.getTokenType())) {
  47                return;
  48            }
  49            // Tokens are minted for one API, which checks that it is the intended audience.
  50            context.getClaims().audience(List.of("brokerage-api"));
  51            // The principal is the signed-in user, or the client itself for client_credentials.
  52            String principal = context.getPrincipal().getName();
  53            String customerId = identities.customers().get(principal);
  54            if (customerId != null) {
  55                context.getClaims().claim("customer_id", customerId);
  56            }
  57            String clientId = context.getRegisteredClient().getClientId();
  58            BigDecimal limit = identities.tradingLimits().get(clientId);
  59            if (limit != null) {
  60                context.getClaims().claim("trading_limit", limit.toPlainString());
  61            }
  62        };
  63    }
  64}

auth-server/src/main/resources/application.yaml64 lines

   1# Development-only authorization server. Plain HTTP, in-memory keys and clients:
   2# never deploy this configuration.
   3server:
   4  port: 9000
   5
   6spring:
   7  application:
   8    name: auth-server
   9  security:
  10    user:
  11      # The demo customer, for the browser-based authorization code flow.
  12      name: alice
  13      password: wonderland
  14    oauth2:
  15      authorizationserver:
  16        issuer: http://localhost:9000
  17        client:
  18          # A customer's own script or trading bot: the "personal API key" pattern.
  19          brokerage-cli:
  20            registration:
  21              client-id: brokerage-cli
  22              client-secret: "{noop}cli-secret"
  23              client-authentication-methods: [client_secret_basic]
  24              authorization-grant-types: [client_credentials]
  25              scopes: [accounts:read, market-data:read, orders:read, orders:write]
  26            token:
  27              access-token-time-to-live: 15m
  28          # The AI agent: same customer, but every order is capped by trading_limit.
  29          brokerage-agent:
  30            registration:
  31              client-id: brokerage-agent
  32              client-secret: "{noop}agent-secret"
  33              client-authentication-methods: [client_secret_basic]
  34              authorization-grant-types: [client_credentials]
  35              scopes: [accounts:read, market-data:read, orders:read, orders:write]
  36            token:
  37              access-token-time-to-live: 5m
  38          # A web app's backend (a "backend for frontend"): a confidential client that signs
  39          # the customer in with the authorization code grant, PKCE and consent. Tokens stay
  40          # on the server; the browser holds only a session cookie. Spring Authorization
  41          # Server issues refresh tokens to confidential clients only.
  42          brokerage-web:
  43            registration:
  44              client-id: brokerage-web
  45              client-secret: "{noop}web-secret"
  46              client-authentication-methods: [client_secret_basic]
  47              authorization-grant-types: [authorization_code, refresh_token]
  48              redirect-uris: [http://127.0.0.1:3000/callback]
  49              scopes: [openid, accounts:read, market-data:read, orders:read, orders:write]
  50            require-proof-key: true
  51            require-authorization-consent: true
  52            token:
  53              access-token-time-to-live: 10m
  54              refresh-token-time-to-live: 8h
  55              reuse-refresh-tokens: false
  56
  57brokerage:
  58  identities:
  59    customers:
  60      alice: cust-1001
  61      brokerage-cli: cust-1001
  62      brokerage-agent: cust-1001
  63    trading-limits:
  64      brokerage-agent: 5000

   1package com.example.brokerage.api;
   2
   3import static org.springframework.hateoas.server.mvc.WebMvcLinkBuilder.linkTo;
   4import static org.springframework.hateoas.server.mvc.WebMvcLinkBuilder.methodOn;
   5
   6import java.time.Duration;
   7
   8import com.example.brokerage.api.accounts.AccountController;
   9import com.example.brokerage.api.market.InstrumentController;
  10
  11import org.springframework.core.io.ClassPathResource;
  12import org.springframework.core.io.Resource;
  13import org.springframework.hateoas.Link;
  14import org.springframework.hateoas.RepresentationModel;
  15import org.springframework.http.CacheControl;
  16import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
  17import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
  18import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;
  19import org.springframework.web.servlet.support.ServletUriComponentsBuilder;
  20
  21/**
  22 * The API root: the one URL a client needs to know. Everything else is discovered by
  23 * following links from here, so the server is free to reorganize every other URI.
  24 */
  25@RestController
  26public class RootController {
  27
  28    /** The root's own properties, beside its links. */
  29    public static class ApiRoot extends RepresentationModel<ApiRoot> {
  30
  31        public final String name = "Brokerage API";
  32        public final String description = "Accounts, positions, market data and trading, as hypermedia";
  33    }
  34
  35    @GetMapping("/")
  36    public ApiRoot root() {
  37        String base = ServletUriComponentsBuilder.fromCurrentContextPath().toUriString();
  38        return new ApiRoot()
  39                .add(linkTo(methodOn(RootController.class).root()).withSelfRel())
  40                .add(linkTo(methodOn(AccountController.class).accounts(null)).withRel("accounts"))
  41                .add(linkTo(methodOn(InstrumentController.class).search(null, null)).withRel("instruments"))
  42                // RFC 8631: the machine-readable description of this API ...
  43                .add(Link.of(base + "/openapi.yaml", "service-desc").withType("application/openapi+yaml"))
  44                // ... and its human-readable documentation.
  45                .add(Link.of("https://docs.brokerage.example", "service-doc").withType("text/html"))
  46                // RFC 9728: where clients learn which authorization server issues tokens for this API.
  47                .add(Link.of(base + "/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource", "oauth-protected-resource"));
  48    }
  49
  50    /** The OpenAPI contract, served by the application it describes so the two ship together. */
  51    @GetMapping(path = "/openapi.yaml", produces = "application/openapi+yaml")
  52    public ResponseEntity<Resource> contract() {
  53        return ResponseEntity.ok()
  54                .cacheControl(CacheControl.maxAge(Duration.ofHours(1)))
  55                .body(new ClassPathResource("contract/brokerage-api.yaml"));
  56    }
  57}

   6/**
   7 * An error the API reports on purpose. It carries its problem type, a detail message for
   8 * the developer, and optional extension members (for example the buying power available).
   9 */
  10public class ApiException extends RuntimeException {
  11
  12    private final ProblemType type;
  13    private final Map<String, Object> extensions = new LinkedHashMap<>();
  14
  15    public ApiException(ProblemType type, String detail) {
  16        super(detail);
  17        this.type = type;
  18    }
  19
  20    public ApiException with(String name, Object value) {
  21        extensions.put(name, value);
  22        return this;
  23    }
  24
  25    public ProblemType type() {
  26        return type;
  27    }
  28
  29    public Map<String, Object> extensions() {
  30        return extensions;
  31    }
  32
  33    public static ApiException notFound(String what, String id) {
  34        return new ApiException(ProblemType.NOT_FOUND, what + " " + id + " was not found");
  35    }
  36}

  13import org.springframework.http.HttpHeaders;
  14import org.springframework.http.HttpStatusCode;
  15import org.springframework.http.ProblemDetail;
  16import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
  17import org.springframework.http.converter.HttpMessageNotReadableException;
  18import org.springframework.security.access.AccessDeniedException;
  19import org.springframework.security.core.AuthenticationException;
  20import org.springframework.web.accept.InvalidApiVersionException;
  21import org.springframework.validation.FieldError;
  22import org.springframework.web.bind.MethodArgumentNotValidException;
  23import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.ExceptionHandler;
  24import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestControllerAdvice;
  25import org.springframework.web.context.request.ServletWebRequest;
  26import org.springframework.web.context.request.WebRequest;
  27import org.springframework.web.servlet.mvc.method.annotation.ResponseEntityExceptionHandler;
  28import tools.jackson.databind.exc.MismatchedInputException;
  29
  30/**
  31 * Turns every error into an RFC 9457 problem document (application/problem+json), with a
  32 * stable type URI, the request path as "instance", and the request ID for support.
  33 * Spring's own exceptions (bad JSON, 405, 406, unsupported versions...) are handled by the
  34 * base class; this class adds the API's catalog and a consistent shape for all of them.
  35 */
  36@RestControllerAdvice
  37public class ApiExceptionHandler extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler {
  38
  39    @ExceptionHandler(ApiException.class)
  40    ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> handleApi(ApiException ex, HttpServletRequest request) {
  41        ProblemDetail problem = problem(ex.type(), ex.getMessage(), request);
  42        ex.extensions().forEach(problem::setProperty);
  43        HttpHeaders headers = new HttpHeaders();
  44        if (ex instanceof RateLimitedException limited) {
  45            headers.set(HttpHeaders.RETRY_AFTER, String.valueOf(limited.retryAfterSeconds()));
  46        }
  47        return ResponseEntity.status(ex.type().status()).headers(headers).body(problem);
  48    }
  49
  50    /** Raised by the security filter chain when no valid token is present. */
  51    @ExceptionHandler(AuthenticationException.class)
  52    ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> handleUnauthenticated(AuthenticationException ex,
  53            HttpServletRequest request) {
  54        return ResponseEntity.status(ProblemType.UNAUTHORIZED.status())
  55                .body(problem(ProblemType.UNAUTHORIZED, "A valid bearer token is required", request));
  56    }
  57
  58    /** Raised when the token is valid but does not carry the scope the operation needs. */
  59    @ExceptionHandler(AccessDeniedException.class)
  60    ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> handleForbidden(AccessDeniedException ex, HttpServletRequest request) {
  61        return ResponseEntity.status(ProblemType.INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE.status())
  62                .body(problem(ProblemType.INSUFFICIENT_SCOPE,
  63                        "The access token does not grant the scope this operation requires", request));
  64    }
  65
  66    /** An API-Version header naming a version this server does not offer. */
  67    @ExceptionHandler(InvalidApiVersionException.class)
  68    ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> handleVersion(InvalidApiVersionException ex, HttpServletRequest request) {
  69        ProblemDetail problem = problem(ProblemType.UNSUPPORTED_API_VERSION,
  70                "API version " + ex.getVersion() + " is not supported", request);
  71        problem.setProperty("supportedVersions", List.of("1", "2"));
  72        return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body(problem);
  73    }
  74
  75    /** Bean Validation failures: one problem, with every invalid field listed. */
  76    @Override
  77    protected ResponseEntity<Object> handleMethodArgumentNotValid(MethodArgumentNotValidException ex,
  78            HttpHeaders headers, HttpStatusCode status, WebRequest request) {
  79        ProblemDetail problem = problem(ProblemType.INVALID_REQUEST, "One or more fields are invalid",
  80                ((ServletWebRequest) request).getRequest());
  81        List<Map<String, String>> errors = ex.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().stream()
  82                .sorted(Comparator.comparing(FieldError::getField))
  83                .map(error -> Map.of("field", error.getField(),
  84                        "message", String.valueOf(error.getDefaultMessage())))
  85                .toList();
  86        problem.setProperty("errors", errors);
  87        return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body(problem);
  88    }
  89
  90    /**
  91     * A body that cannot be read: malformed JSON, or a value of the wrong type such as an
  92     * unknown enum constant. A wrong value is reported in the same "errors" shape as a
  93     * Bean Validation failure, so clients handle one format for every invalid field.
  94     */
  95    @Override
  96    protected ResponseEntity<Object> handleHttpMessageNotReadable(HttpMessageNotReadableException ex,
  97            HttpHeaders headers, HttpStatusCode status, WebRequest request) {
  98        HttpServletRequest servletRequest = ((ServletWebRequest) request).getRequest();
  99        for (Throwable cause = ex; cause != null; cause = cause.getCause()) {
 100            if (cause instanceof MismatchedInputException mismatch && !mismatch.getPath().isEmpty()) {
 101                ProblemDetail problem = problem(ProblemType.INVALID_REQUEST, "One or more fields are invalid",
 102                        servletRequest);
 103                problem.setProperty("errors", List.of(Map.of("field", fieldPath(mismatch),
 104                        "message", expected(mismatch.getTargetType()))));
 105                return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body(problem);
 106            }
 107        }
 108        return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body(problem(ProblemType.INVALID_REQUEST,
 109                "The request body is not valid JSON", servletRequest));
 110    }
 111
 112    private static String fieldPath(MismatchedInputException mismatch) {
 113        return mismatch.getPath().stream()
 114                .map(ref -> ref.getPropertyName() != null ? ref.getPropertyName()
 115                        : "[" + ref.getIndex() + "]")
 116                .collect(Collectors.joining("."));
 117    }
 118
 119    private static String expected(Class<?> type) {
 120        if (type != null && type.isEnum()) {
 121            return "must be one of " + Arrays.stream(type.getEnumConstants()).map(Object::toString)
 122                    .collect(Collectors.joining(", "));
 123        }
 124        return type == BigDecimal.class ? "must be a decimal number written as a string, such as \"10.25\""
 125                : "has the wrong type";
 126    }
 127
 128    /** Everything Spring raises itself gets the same instance and requestId members. */
 129    @Override
 130    protected ResponseEntity<Object> createResponseEntity(Object body, HttpHeaders headers,
 131            HttpStatusCode status, WebRequest request) {
 132        if (body instanceof ProblemDetail problem) {
 133            HttpServletRequest servletRequest = ((ServletWebRequest) request).getRequest();
 134            if (problem.getType() == null || "about:blank".equals(problem.getType().toString())) {
 135                problem.setType(URI.create(ProblemType.BASE + slugFor(status)));
 136            }
 137            problem.setInstance(URI.create(servletRequest.getRequestURI()));
 138            problem.setProperty("requestId", RequestIdFilter.currentId(servletRequest));
 139        }
 140        return super.createResponseEntity(body, headers, status, request);
 141    }
 142
 143    static ProblemDetail problem(ProblemType type, String detail, HttpServletRequest request) {
 144        ProblemDetail problem = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(type.status(), detail);
 145        problem.setType(type.uri());
 146        problem.setTitle(type.title());
 147        problem.setInstance(URI.create(request.getRequestURI()));
 148        problem.setProperty("requestId", RequestIdFilter.currentId(request));
 149        return problem;
 150    }
 151
 152    private static String slugFor(HttpStatusCode status) {
 153        return switch (status.value()) {
 154            case 400 -> "invalid-request";
 155            case 404 -> "not-found";
 156            case 405 -> "method-not-allowed";
 157            case 406 -> "not-acceptable";
 158            case 415 -> "unsupported-media-type";
 159            default -> "http-" + status.value();
 160        };
 161    }
 162}

   1package com.example.brokerage.api.platform;

   3import java.math.BigDecimal;

   6import java.util.Optional;

   8import org.springframework.security.oauth2.jwt.Jwt;
   9
  10/**
  11 * Who is calling, as established by the access token: the customer whose data may be
  12 * read, the client application acting for them, what it may do, and any trading limit
  13 * the customer delegated to that client.
  14 */
  15public record Caller(String customerId, String clientId, Collection<String> scopes,
  16        Optional<BigDecimal> tradingLimit) {
  17
  18    public static Caller of(Jwt jwt) {
  19        // A valid token that is not bound to a customer can see no accounts at all.
  20        String customerId = Optional.ofNullable(jwt.getClaimAsString("customer_id")).orElse("none");
  21        // "scope" may be a space-delimited string (RFC 6749) or a JSON array.
  22        Collection<String> scopes = jwt.getClaim("scope") instanceof String text
  23                ? List.of(text.split(" "))
  24                : Optional.ofNullable(jwt.getClaimAsStringList("scope")).orElse(List.of());
  25        Optional<BigDecimal> limit = Optional.ofNullable(jwt.getClaimAsString("trading_limit"))
  26                .map(BigDecimal::new);
  27        return new Caller(customerId, jwt.getSubject(), scopes, limit);
  28    }
  29
  30    public boolean canTrade() {
  31        return scopes.contains("orders:write");
  32    }
  33
  34    public boolean canReadOrders() {
  35        return scopes.contains("orders:read");
  36    }
  37}

   1package com.example.brokerage.api.platform;
   2
   3import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
   4import java.time.Instant;
   5import java.util.Base64;
   6import java.util.Comparator;
   7import java.util.List;
   8import java.util.function.Function;
   9
  10/**
  11 * One page of a newest-first list, with an opaque cursor for the next page.
  12 *
  13 * <p>The cursor encodes the sort key (timestamp and ID) of the last item returned, so a
  14 * page never skips or repeats items when new ones are inserted at the top: something
  15 * offset-based paging ("page=3") cannot promise. Clients never parse cursors; they
  16 * follow the "next" link that carries one.
  17 */
  18public record CursorPage<T>(List<T> items, String nextCursor) {
  19
  20    public static final int DEFAULT_LIMIT = 25;
  21    public static final int MAX_LIMIT = 100;
  22
  23    public boolean hasNext() {
  24        return nextCursor != null;
  25    }
  26
  27    public static <T> CursorPage<T> of(List<T> all, Function<T, Instant> time, Function<T, String> id,
  28            String cursor, Integer requestedLimit) {
  29        int limit = requestedLimit == null ? DEFAULT_LIMIT : requestedLimit;
  30        if (limit < 1 || limit > MAX_LIMIT) {
  31            throw new ApiException(ProblemType.INVALID_REQUEST,
  32                    "limit must be between 1 and " + MAX_LIMIT);
  33        }
  34        Comparator<T> newestFirst = Comparator.comparing(time).thenComparing(id).reversed();
  35        List<T> sorted = all.stream().sorted(newestFirst).toList();
  36
  37        int start = 0;
  38        if (cursor != null) {
  39            Key after = Key.decode(cursor);
  40            while (start < sorted.size() && !isOlder(sorted.get(start), after, time, id)) {
  41                start++;
  42            }
  43        }
  44        int end = Math.min(start + limit, sorted.size());
  45        List<T> items = sorted.subList(start, end);
  46        String next = end < sorted.size()
  47                ? new Key(time.apply(items.getLast()), id.apply(items.getLast())).encode()
  48                : null;
  49        return new CursorPage<>(items, next);
  50    }
  51
  52    private static <T> boolean isOlder(T item, Key after, Function<T, Instant> time, Function<T, String> id) {
  53        int byTime = time.apply(item).compareTo(after.time());
  54        return byTime < 0 || (byTime == 0 && id.apply(item).compareTo(after.id()) < 0);
  55    }
  56
  57    record Key(Instant time, String id) {
  58
  59        String encode() {
  60            String raw = time.toEpochMilli() + ":" + id;
  61            return Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding()
  62                    .encodeToString(raw.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
  63        }
  64
  65        static Key decode(String cursor) {
  66            try {
  67                String raw = new String(Base64.getUrlDecoder().decode(cursor), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
  68                int colon = raw.indexOf(':');
  69                return new Key(Instant.ofEpochMilli(Long.parseLong(raw.substring(0, colon))),
  70                        raw.substring(colon + 1));
  71            } catch (RuntimeException ex) {
  72                throw new ApiException(ProblemType.INVALID_REQUEST, "The cursor is malformed or expired");
  73            }
  74        }
  75    }
  76}

   1package com.example.brokerage.api.platform;
   2
   3import java.math.BigDecimal;
   4import java.util.Set;
   5
   6import com.example.brokerage.api.orders.Order;
   7import com.example.brokerage.api.orders.OrderRequest;
   8
   9import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
  10import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
  11import org.springframework.hateoas.LinkRelation;
  12import org.springframework.hateoas.UriTemplate;
  13import org.springframework.hateoas.config.EnableHypermediaSupport;
  14import org.springframework.hateoas.config.EnableHypermediaSupport.HypermediaType;
  15import org.springframework.hateoas.mediatype.hal.CurieProvider;
  16import org.springframework.hateoas.mediatype.hal.DefaultCurieProvider;
  17import org.springframework.hateoas.mediatype.hal.HalLinkRelation;
  18import org.springframework.hateoas.mediatype.hal.forms.HalFormsConfiguration;
  19import org.springframework.hateoas.mediatype.hal.forms.HalFormsOptions;
  20
  21/**
  22 * Hypermedia formats and link relations.
  23 *
  24 * <p>HAL (application/hal+json) is the default. Clients that ask for HAL-FORMS
  25 * (application/prs.hal-forms+json) also receive "_templates": machine-readable
  26 * descriptions of the state transitions available right now, such as placing,
  27 * changing or canceling an order.
  28 */
  29@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
  30@EnableHypermediaSupport(type = { HypermediaType.HAL, HypermediaType.HAL_FORMS })
  31public class HypermediaConfig {
  32
  33    /** Documentation for every custom link relation lives at this URI template. */
  34    public static final String RELS = "https://docs.brokerage.example/rels/{rel}";
  35
  36    /**
  37     * Relations that are not registered with IANA (like "orders") are custom, and HAL
  38     * requires custom relations to be URIs. A CURIE keeps them short on the wire:
  39     * "bk:orders" expands to https://docs.brokerage.example/rels/orders.
  40     */
  41    @Bean
  42    CurieProvider curieProvider() {
  43        return new DefaultCurieProvider("bk", UriTemplate.of(RELS)) {
  44            @Override
  45            public HalLinkRelation getNamespacedRelFor(LinkRelation relation) {
  46                // Registered by RFC 8631, but missing from Spring HATEOAS's list of IANA relations.
  47                return RFC_8631.contains(relation.value()) ? HalLinkRelation.uncuried(relation.value())
  48                        : super.getNamespacedRelFor(relation);
  49            }
  50        };
  51    }
  52
  53    private static final Set<String> RFC_8631 = Set.of("service-desc", "service-doc", "service-meta");
  54
  55    /** Offer the allowed values of enum fields inside HAL-FORMS templates. */
  56    @Bean
  57    HalFormsConfiguration halFormsConfiguration() {
  58        return new HalFormsConfiguration()
  59                // Decimals travel as strings: describe them as text that must look like a number.
  60                .withPattern(BigDecimal.class, "^[0-9]+(\\.[0-9]+)?$")
  61                .withOptions(OrderRequest.class, "side",
  62                        metadata -> HalFormsOptions.inline(Order.Side.values()))
  63                .withOptions(OrderRequest.class, "type",
  64                        metadata -> HalFormsOptions.inline(Order.Type.values()))
  65                .withOptions(OrderRequest.class, "timeInForce",
  66                        metadata -> HalFormsOptions.inline(Order.TimeInForce.values()));
  67    }
  68}

   1package com.example.brokerage.api.platform;
   2
   3import java.math.BigDecimal;
   4
   5import com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonFormat;
   6
   7import org.springframework.boot.jackson.autoconfigure.JsonMapperBuilderCustomizer;
   8import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
   9import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
  10
  11/**
  12 * JSON conventions that apply to every representation.
  13 */
  14@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
  15public class JsonConfig {
  16
  17    /**
  18     * Money, prices and quantities are written as decimal strings ("187.50"), never as
  19     * JSON numbers. Many JSON parsers read numbers into binary floating point, where
  20     * 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3; a string survives every parser intact.
  21     */
  22    @Bean
  23    JsonMapperBuilderCustomizer decimalsAsStrings() {
  24        return builder -> builder.withConfigOverride(BigDecimal.class,
  25                override -> override.setFormat(JsonFormat.Value.forShape(JsonFormat.Shape.STRING)));
  26    }
  27}
